// invisible to the caller — looks like a normal assignment\n return true;\n },\n });\n}\n\nconst state = reactive({ count: 0 }, (prop, value) => console.log(`${prop} changed to ${value}`));\nstate.count++; // logs \"count changed to 1\"" }, "reference": { "label": "Proxy — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Proxy" } }, { "id": "q-js-024", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "What is `for await...of`, and what problem does it solve when consuming an async iterable?", "answer": "`for await...of` iterates over an async iterable — a source that produces a sequence of Promises (or values wrapped as such), commonly a stream of paginated API results or a `ReadableStream` — automatically `await`ing each yielded value before running the loop body, rather than requiring you to manually `await` each item yourself inside a regular loop.\n\nWithout it, consuming something like an async generator that yields pages of results would require manually calling `.next()` and `await`ing each result in a hand-rolled loop; `for await...of` gives the same natural, readable iteration syntax as a synchronous `for...of` loop while correctly sequencing the asynchronous waits, which matters especially for streaming APIs where you want to process each chunk as it arrives rather than waiting for the entire stream to buffer first.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "async function* fetchPages(url) {\n while (url) {\n const res = await fetch(url);\n const page = await res.json();\n yield page.items;\n url = page.nextUrl;\n }\n}\n\nfor await (const items of fetchPages(\"/api/results\")) {\n console.log(items); // each page processed as soon as it arrives\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "for await...of — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of" } }, { "id": "q-js-025", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "At a high level, how does mark-and-sweep garbage collection work in JavaScript engines, and why doesn't reference counting alone suffice?", "answer": "Mark-and-sweep starts from a set of \"roots\" (global objects, currently executing call stack) and marks every object reachable from those roots by walking references transitively; anything left unmarked after that traversal is considered garbage and swept (its memory reclaimed) — reachability, not reference count, is what determines whether an object survives.\n\nSimple reference counting (reclaiming an object the instant its reference count hits zero) fails on circular references: two objects that reference each other but are otherwise unreachable from any root would each show a reference count of one forever, never reaching zero, and would leak indefinitely under pure reference counting. Mark-and-sweep correctly identifies such a cycle as garbage because neither object is reachable from a root, regardless of how many references point to each other internally.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "let a = {}; let b = {};\na.ref = b; b.ref = a; // circular reference, ref count 1 each\na = null; b = null; // no longer reachable from any root\n\n// Mark-and-sweep: neither object is reachable from a root -> both collected\n// Pure reference counting: both counts stay at 1 forever -> leaked" }, "reference": { "label": "Memory management — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Memory_management" } }, { "id": "q-js-026", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "Why does `[] + []` produce an empty string, and `[] + {}` produce `\"[object Object]\"` — what coercion rules explain this?", "answer": "The `+` operator, when neither operand is already a number, converts both operands to primitives first (calling `toString()` if no `Symbol.toPrimitive`/`valueOf` short-circuits it), then concatenates if either result is a string. An array's default `toString()` joins its elements with commas — an empty array becomes `\"\"` — so `[] + []` becomes `\"\" + \"\"`, which is `\"\"`.\n\nA plain object's default `toString()` produces the literal string `\"[object Object]\"` (from `Object.prototype.toString`, unless overridden), so `[] + {}` becomes `\"\" + \"[object Object]\"`, which is `\"[object Object]\"`. These aren't special-cased rules for arrays/objects specifically — they're just the general \"convert to primitive, then string-concatenate\" behavior of `+` applied to each type's own particular `toString()` implementation, which is why memorizing the underlying coercion algorithm explains far more of these quirks than memorizing individual cases.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "console.log([] + []); // \"\" -> \"\".toString() + \"\".toString()\nconsole.log([] + {}); // \"[object Object]\" -> \"\" + \"[object Object]\"\nconsole.log({} + []); // varies by context — same underlying toString() coercion rules apply" }, "reference": { "label": "Type coercion — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Data_structures" } }, { "id": "q-js-027", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "What's the difference between function hoisting and `var` hoisting, and why can you call a function declaration before the line it's written on but not a function expression assigned to a `var`?", "answer": "A function *declaration* (`function foo() {}`) is hoisted completely — both its name and its entire body are available at the top of the enclosing scope, so calling it before its literal position in the source works fine. A `var` holding a function *expression* (`var foo = function() {}`) only has the `var` declaration itself hoisted (initialized to `undefined`); the assignment of the function to it still happens in place, at its original line — calling `foo()` before that line throws, because `foo` is still `undefined` at that point, not yet a function.\n\nThis distinction is a common source of confusion precisely because both look similar at a glance but hoist completely differently — relying on function declaration hoisting for genuine forward-reference cases is fine and idiomatic, but relying on it as a substitute for understanding execution order is a frequent source of \"works when I move this line\" bugs.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "sayHi(); // works — function declarations hoist fully\nfunction sayHi() { console.log(\"hi\"); }\n\nsayBye(); // TypeError: sayBye is not a function\nvar sayBye = function () { console.log(\"bye\"); }; // only the 'var' hoists, as undefined" }, "reference": { "label": "Function hoisting — MDN Glossary", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Hoisting" } }, { "id": "q-js-028", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "Why does firing off multiple `await`s sequentially inside a loop hurt performance compared to `Promise.all`, when the operations don't depend on each other?", "answer": "`for (const id of ids) { await fetchThing(id); }` awaits each fetch to fully complete before even starting the next one — if each fetch takes 200ms and there are 10 IDs, the total time is roughly 2 seconds, even though nothing about fetch #2 actually depends on fetch #1 finishing first.\n\nStarting all the promises first (`const promises = ids.map(id => fetchThing(id))`) and then awaiting them together (`await Promise.all(promises)`) lets every request run concurrently, so the total time is roughly bounded by the single *slowest* request rather than the sum of all of them — the sequential-await-in-a-loop pattern is one of the most common accidental performance bugs in async JavaScript, especially since it reads perfectly reasonably and produces correct (just needlessly slow) results.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "// Slow: ~200ms * 10 = ~2000ms total, sequential\nfor (const id of ids) {\n const result = await fetchThing(id);\n}\n\n// Fast: all requests run concurrently, bounded by the slowest one (~200ms)\nconst results = await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => fetchThing(id)));" }, "reference": { "label": "Promise.all() — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all" } }, { "id": "q-js-029", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "What does JavaScript's \"strict mode\" (`'use strict'`) actually change, and why is it the implicit default inside ES modules and classes?", "answer": "Strict mode turns several previously-silent mistakes into thrown errors — assigning to an undeclared variable (which would otherwise silently create an accidental global), assigning to a read-only property, duplicate parameter names — and changes `this` inside a plain function call from the global object to `undefined`, surfacing bugs that non-strict mode would otherwise hide or silently misbehave on.\n\nES modules and `class` bodies are automatically strict mode with no `'use strict'` directive needed, reflecting that strict mode's stricter, more predictable behavior is simply considered the correct default for modern code — the looser, more permissive legacy behavior is preserved only for older, non-module script code for backward compatibility, not because it's considered preferable going forward.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "function loose() { undeclaredVar = 5; } // silently creates a global — no error\nloose();\n\nfunction strict() {\n \"use strict\";\n undeclaredVar2 = 5; // ReferenceError — caught immediately\n}\n\n// Inside a module or class body, strict mode is implicit — no directive needed\nexport class Example { method() { /* already strict */ } }" }, "reference": { "label": "Strict mode — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Strict_mode" } }, { "id": "q-js-030", "category": "JavaScript", "question": "What's the difference between event bubbling and event capturing, and which one does `addEventListener` use by default?", "answer": "When an event fires on a nested element, it travels in two phases: capturing goes from the outermost ancestor down to the actual target element, and bubbling goes back from the target up through its ancestors again. Most native DOM event handling code only ever deals with the bubbling phase, since `addEventListener`'s third argument (whether to use capturing) defaults to `false`, meaning listeners fire during the bubble-up phase by default.\n\nExplicitly passing `true` (or `{capture: true}`) registers a listener for the capturing phase instead, which runs *before* the event ever reaches the actual target — useful in specific cases where a parent needs to intercept or short-circuit an event before a child's own handler gets a chance to run (e.g. `event.stopPropagation()` called during capture prevents the event from ever reaching the target or bubbling at all).", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "parent.addEventListener(\"click\", () => console.log(\"bubble phase\")); // default: bubbling\nparent.addEventListener(\"click\", () => console.log(\"capture phase\"), { capture: true }); // runs first\n\nchild.addEventListener(\"click\", (e) => {\n console.log(\"target\");\n // e.stopPropagation(); // would stop this from ever reaching the bubble-phase listener above\n});" }, "reference": { "label": "Event capture, propagation, and bubbling — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/Scripting/Event_bubbling" } }, { "id": "q-ts-001", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is structural typing in TypeScript, and how is it fundamentally different from the nominal typing found in languages like C# or Java?", "answer": "In a nominally-typed language, two types are compatible only if one explicitly declares itself as implementing/extending the other, regardless of whether their members happen to match. TypeScript uses structural typing instead: a value is considered compatible with a type if it *has the right shape* — the right properties and method signatures — even if it was never declared to implement that interface at all.\n\nThis means two entirely unrelated interfaces with identical member signatures are freely interchangeable in TypeScript, which surprises developers coming from nominally-typed backgrounds; it also means an object literal or class satisfies an interface purely by having compatible members, no `implements` keyword required — the type checker cares about \"does this look like the right shape,\" not \"was this explicitly declared as this type.\"", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface HasName { name: string; }\n\nfunction greet(entity: HasName) { console.log(\"Hi \" + entity.name); }\n\nclass Dog { constructor(public name: string) {} } // never \"implements HasName\"\ngreet(new Dog(\"Rex\")); // fine — shape matches\ngreet({ name: \"Ad-hoc object\" }); // also fine — no declared relationship needed" }, "reference": { "label": "Type Compatibility — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/type-compatibility.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-002", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "When would you choose an `interface` over a `type` alias in TypeScript, given how much overlap they have?", "answer": "Both can describe an object's shape and are largely interchangeable for that purpose, but they diverge in a few concrete ways: interfaces support declaration merging (declaring the same interface name twice in different places merges their members into one), which type aliases cannot do at all, and interfaces are generally the conventional choice for public API surfaces that consumers might want to extend. Type aliases, on the other hand, can represent things an interface fundamentally cannot — union types, tuple types, mapped/conditional types.\n\nA common practical convention: use `interface` for object shapes you expect to be extended or implemented by classes, and `type` for everything else (unions, primitives, function signatures, complex derived/mapped types) — though many codebases simply pick one as a house style for plain object shapes and reserve `type` specifically for the cases only it can express.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface User { id: string; name: string; } // extendable object shape\ninterface Admin extends User { role: \"admin\"; }\n\ntype Status = \"pending\" | \"active\" | \"closed\"; // a type alias can express a union\ntype Handler = (event: Event) => void; // ...or a function signature" }, "reference": { "label": "Interfaces vs. Type Aliases — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#differences-between-type-aliases-and-interfaces" } }, { "id": "q-ts-003", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What problem do generics solve in TypeScript, and what's the difference between a function using `any` and one using a generic type parameter?", "answer": "`function first(arr: any[]): any` compiles and \"works\" for any array, but it throws away all type information — the caller gets back `any`, meaning no compile-time safety on what they do with the result, and the type checker can't catch a mismatch between what was passed in and what's expected downstream.\n\n`function first(arr: T[]): T` preserves the relationship between the input and output types — calling it with `string[]` gives back a `string`, with full autocomplete and type-checking on whatever you do with that result, without needing to write a separate overload for every possible element type. Generics let you write one function that works across many types while the type checker still verifies the *relationships* between those types are preserved correctly — `any` gives up that verification entirely.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "function firstAny(arr: any[]): any { return arr[0]; }\nconst x = firstAny([\"a\", \"b\"]); // x: any — no safety on what you do next\n\nfunction firstGeneric(arr: T[]): T { return arr[0]; }\nconst y = firstGeneric([\"a\", \"b\"]); // y: string — inferred and checked" }, "reference": { "label": "Generics — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-004", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the difference between a union type and an intersection type, and how would you use each in a real API design?", "answer": "A union type (`A | B`) means a value could be *either* type — you can only safely access members common to both without first narrowing which one it actually is. An intersection type (`A & B`) means a value must satisfy *both* types simultaneously — it combines all their members into a single required shape.\n\nA real example: modeling API responses, you might use a union (`SuccessResponse | ErrorResponse`) to represent that a call resolves to one or the other, requiring a discriminant check before accessing response-specific fields; you might use an intersection (`BaseEntity & { role: 'admin' }`) to extend a shared base shape with additional required fields for a more specific variant, when every instance genuinely needs all of both sets of properties at once.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "type SuccessResponse = { ok: true; data: string };\ntype ErrorResponse = { ok: false; error: string };\ntype ApiResponse = SuccessResponse | ErrorResponse; // could be either\n\ntype BaseEntity = { id: string; createdAt: string };\ntype AdminUser = BaseEntity & { role: \"admin\" }; // must have both" }, "reference": { "label": "Union and Intersection Types — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#union-and-intersection-types-in-object-types" } }, { "id": "q-ts-005", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is a discriminated union in TypeScript, and how does it make a `switch` statement exhaustive and safe?", "answer": "A discriminated union is a union of object types that all share one common literal property (a \"discriminant\" or \"tag,\" e.g. `kind: 'circle' | 'square'`) with a distinct literal value per variant — checking that one property (`if (shape.kind === 'circle')`) lets TypeScript narrow the value to the exact matching variant, safely exposing only that variant's specific properties within that branch.\n\nCombined with a `never`-typed exhaustiveness check in a `switch`'s `default` case (assigning the unhandled value to a variable typed `never`), TypeScript will raise a compile error if a new variant is added to the union later but a corresponding `case` is never added to handle it — turning a runtime \"forgot to handle the new case\" bug into an immediate compile-time error instead.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "type Shape =\n | { kind: \"circle\"; radius: number }\n | { kind: \"square\"; side: number };\n\nfunction area(shape: Shape): number {\n switch (shape.kind) {\n case \"circle\": return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;\n case \"square\": return shape.side ** 2;\n default:\n const exhaustive: never = shape; // compile error if a new variant is added and unhandled\n throw new Error(\"Unhandled shape\");\n }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Discriminated Unions — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#discriminated-unions" } }, { "id": "q-ts-006", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the practical difference between `unknown` and `any`, and why is `unknown` considered the safer choice for representing genuinely untyped input?", "answer": "`any` opts a value out of type checking entirely — you can call any method, access any property, assign it to anything, with zero compiler safety net, and that lack of safety can silently spread to anything the `any` value touches. `unknown` also represents \"could be anything,\" but the compiler refuses to let you do *anything* with an `unknown` value (call a method, access a property, pass it somewhere requiring a specific type) until you've first narrowed it via a type guard or assertion.\n\nThis makes `unknown` the correct type for genuinely unpredictable input — the result of `JSON.parse`, a value from an external API — because it forces the code that receives it to actually validate/narrow its shape before using it, rather than silently trusting an assumption that might be wrong; `any` would let that same unsafe assumption compile without complaint.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "function handleAny(value: any) { value.toUpperCase(); } // compiles, may crash at runtime\n\nfunction handleUnknown(value: unknown) {\n // value.toUpperCase(); // compile error — must narrow first\n if (typeof value === \"string\") value.toUpperCase(); // fine after the guard\n}\n\nconst parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(rawInput); // correct type for untrusted input" }, "reference": { "label": "unknown Type — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-0.html#the-unknown-type" } }, { "id": "q-ts-007", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is the `never` type used for, and where does it show up that isn't just \"a function that always throws\"?", "answer": "`never` represents a value that can genuinely never occur — a function that always throws or never returns has a return type of `never` (not `void`, which means \"returns nothing meaningful\" but still returns), and it's also what a variable's type narrows to inside a branch the type checker has proven is unreachable.\n\nBeyond the throwing-function case, `never` is the standard tool for exhaustiveness checking in a discriminated union `switch`: assigning the value in an unhandled `default` branch to a variable explicitly typed `never` only compiles if the type checker has actually narrowed every other case away, meaning if a new union variant is added later without updating the switch, that assignment stops compiling — deliberately using `never`'s \"this should be impossible\" meaning as a compile-time completeness check.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "function fail(message: string): never { throw new Error(message); } // never returns\n\ntype Shape = { kind: \"circle\" } | { kind: \"square\" };\nfunction area(s: Shape) {\n if (s.kind === \"circle\") return 1;\n if (s.kind === \"square\") return 2;\n const check: never = s; // stops compiling if a new \"kind\" is added without a branch here\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "never Type — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#never" } }, { "id": "q-ts-008", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What do `Partial`, `Pick`, and `Omit` do, and what's a practical case for each?", "answer": "`Partial` makes every property of `T` optional — useful for an \"update\" function signature where a caller may supply only the fields they want to change, rather than the entire object. `Pick` constructs a new type containing only the specified subset of `T`'s properties — useful for deriving a narrower view type (a summary/list-row shape) from a larger, canonical entity type without redeclaring those fields separately.\n\n`Omit` is the inverse of `Pick` — every property of `T` except the ones named — commonly used to derive a \"create\" input type from an entity type by excluding server-generated fields like `id` or `createdAt` that a client should never be allowed to supply. All three derive a new type mechanically from an existing one, which keeps related types in sync automatically as the base type evolves, rather than maintaining several independently hand-written, easily-drifting variants.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; createdAt: string; }\n\nfunction updateUser(id: string, changes: Partial) { /* only supplied fields required */ }\n\ntype UserSummary = Pick; // narrower view type\ntype CreateUserInput = Omit; // exclude server-generated fields" }, "reference": { "label": "Utility Types — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-009", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the difference between a TypeScript `enum` and a union of string literals, and why do many teams prefer the latter?", "answer": "A numeric `enum` compiles to actual runtime JavaScript code — an object mapping names to numbers and back — adding real bytes to the output bundle and a real runtime construct, whereas a union of string literals (`type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'closed'`) is purely a compile-time construct that's completely erased, adding zero runtime footprint.\n\nString literal unions also serialize and debug more transparently (the actual value in a log or JSON payload is the readable string `'active'`, not an opaque number that requires looking up the enum definition to interpret), and they avoid a specific numeric-enum footgun where any number is assignable to a numeric enum type by default, defeating some of the type safety the enum was meant to provide. `const enum` addresses the runtime-footprint concern by inlining values at compile time, but many teams simply standardize on string literal unions to sidestep the tradeoffs entirely.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "enum StatusEnum { Pending, Active, Closed } // compiles to a real runtime object\n\ntype Status = \"pending\" | \"active\" | \"closed\"; // erased entirely, zero runtime footprint\n\nfunction setStatus(s: Status) { console.log(s); } // logs the readable string, not a number\nsetStatus(\"active\");" }, "reference": { "label": "Enums — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/enums.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-010", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What does `readonly` actually enforce in TypeScript, and what's the difference between `readonly` on a property versus using `Readonly` or `ReadonlyArray`?", "answer": "`readonly` on a property (or `Readonly` applied to a whole type) prevents *reassignment* of that property after the object is created, at the type-checker level — attempting `obj.prop = newValue` on a readonly property is a compile error. It's purely a compile-time restriction: nothing about `readonly` changes the underlying JavaScript at runtime, so a function that receives the same object through a differently-typed (non-readonly) reference can still mutate it freely, and there's no runtime enforcement (like `Object.freeze` provides) at all.\n\n`ReadonlyArray` (or `readonly T[]`) similarly blocks mutating array methods (`push`, `splice`, direct index assignment) at the type level, forcing code to produce new arrays rather than mutate in place — useful for signaling and enforcing immutable-by-convention data flow through the type system, even though it's the type checker, not the runtime, doing the enforcing.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface Point { readonly x: number; readonly y: number; }\nconst p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 };\n// p.x = 5; // compile error\n\nconst nums: ReadonlyArray = [1, 2, 3];\n// nums.push(4); // compile error — but Object.freeze(nums) would be needed for real runtime enforcement" }, "reference": { "label": "readonly — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#readonly-properties" } }, { "id": "q-ts-011", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is declaration merging in TypeScript, and what's a legitimate use case for it?", "answer": "Declaration merging lets you declare the same name (an interface, a namespace) multiple times in different places, and TypeScript combines all the declarations into a single merged definition rather than treating the second one as a conflicting redeclaration or an error.\n\nA legitimate, common use case is augmenting a third-party library's types — e.g. extending Express's `Request` interface (declared by the `@types/express` package) in your own project's ambient declaration file to add a custom `req.user` property your auth middleware attaches, without needing to fork or patch the library's own type definitions. Without merging, adding properties to a type you don't own and can't edit directly would require an awkward type assertion at every usage site instead of one centralized declaration.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "// your-project/types/express/index.d.ts\ndeclare namespace Express {\n interface Request {\n user?: { id: string; roles: string[] }; // merges into the library's own Request interface\n }\n}\n\n// now usable anywhere without a cast:\napp.use((req, res, next) => { console.log(req.user?.id); next(); });" }, "reference": { "label": "Declaration Merging — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-merging.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-012", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is a mapped type, and how does `Partial` actually work under the hood as one?", "answer": "A mapped type produces a new type by iterating over the keys of an existing type and transforming each property according to a rule — `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` copies every property as-is, and modifiers can be applied during that iteration to change optionality or readonly-ness for every property uniformly.\n\n`Partial` is defined (in TypeScript's own standard library) essentially as `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }` — it iterates every key of `T` and adds the `?` optional modifier to each, which is exactly why it works generically for *any* object type without needing a separate hand-written \"partial version\" of every interface in your codebase; the mapped type mechanically derives it from whatever `T` you apply it to.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "type MyPartial = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }; // essentially how Partial is defined\n\ninterface User { id: string; name: string; }\ntype PartialUser = MyPartial; // { id?: string; name?: string; }" }, "reference": { "label": "Mapped Types — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-013", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is a conditional type, and what does the `infer` keyword let you do inside one?", "answer": "A conditional type (`T extends U ? X : Y`) resolves to one of two types depending on whether `T` is assignable to `U` — a type-level if/else that lets a generic type's shape depend on what it's instantiated with, rather than being fixed.\n\n`infer` lets you *capture* a type from within the structure being checked, for use in the resulting branch — e.g. `type ReturnTypeOf = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never` extracts a function's actual return type by pattern-matching against the shape \"a function returning something\" and binding that \"something\" to `R`. This is how many of TypeScript's own built-in utility types (`ReturnType`, `Parameters`) are implemented — deriving one type from the internal structure of another, entirely at compile time.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "type ReturnTypeOf = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;\n\nfunction getUser() { return { id: \"1\", name: \"Alice\" }; }\ntype User = ReturnTypeOf; // { id: string; name: string }" }, "reference": { "label": "Conditional Types — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-014", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "How do function overloads work in TypeScript, and why can't you just use a union type parameter instead?", "answer": "Overloads declare multiple call signatures for the same function name, each specifying a distinct combination of parameter and return types, followed by one actual implementation signature broad enough to satisfy all of them — callers see only the specific overload signatures, and TypeScript picks the matching one based on the arguments actually passed at each call site.\n\nA union parameter type (`function f(x: string | number): string | number`) can express \"accepts either,\" but it can't express a *precise correlation* between input and output — that passing a `string` specifically returns a `string`, and passing a `number` specifically returns a `number`. Overloads let each declared signature pin down that exact input-to-output relationship per case, which a single unioned signature collapses into a less precise \"could be either\" for both the parameter and the return type.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "function parse(value: string): string;\nfunction parse(value: number): number;\nfunction parse(value: string | number): string | number {\n return typeof value === \"string\" ? value.trim() : value * 2;\n}\n\nconst a = parse(\"hi\"); // a: string\nconst b = parse(5); // b: number — precise per overload, unlike a plain union signature" }, "reference": { "label": "Function Overloads — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#function-overloads" } }, { "id": "q-ts-015", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What does enabling `strictNullChecks` actually change, and why is it usually the single highest-value compiler flag to turn on?", "answer": "Without `strictNullChecks`, `null` and `undefined` are assignable to essentially every type, meaning the compiler can't help you catch a missing null check at all — any variable could silently be `null` at runtime with zero compile-time warning. With it enabled, `null`/`undefined` are only assignable to types that explicitly include them (`string | null`), so accessing a property on a possibly-null value without first narrowing it out is a compile error.\n\nIt's usually the highest-value flag specifically because \"cannot read property of undefined/null\" is one of the single most common runtime crash classes in JavaScript codebases, and this flag converts a large fraction of those from a runtime crash discovered in production into a compile-time error caught before the code ever ships — most of TypeScript's other strictness flags catch narrower classes of bugs than this one does.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "// tsconfig.json: { \"compilerOptions\": { \"strictNullChecks\": true } }\n\nfunction getLength(s: string | null): number {\n // return s.length; // compile error — s might be null\n return s?.length ?? 0; // must narrow or handle it first\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "strictNullChecks — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strictNullChecks" } }, { "id": "q-ts-016", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is a `.d.ts` declaration file, and why does a plain JavaScript library need one to be usable safely from TypeScript?", "answer": "A `.d.ts` file describes the types of a module's exports — function signatures, object shapes, generic parameters — without containing any actual runtime implementation at all; it's purely type information layered on top of existing JavaScript code that the type checker otherwise has no way to understand.\n\nWithout one, importing a plain JS library gives you either a compile error (in strict setups) or an implicit `any` type for everything it exports, losing all type checking and autocomplete for that library's API entirely. Popular libraries either ship their own `.d.ts` files alongside their JS code, or the community maintains them separately (the `@types/*` packages on npm, sourced from the DefinitelyTyped project) precisely so consumers get full type safety against a library that itself was never written in TypeScript.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "// legacy-lib.d.ts\ndeclare module \"legacy-lib\" {\n export function formatDate(input: string, pattern: string): string;\n}\n\nimport { formatDate } from \"legacy-lib\"; // fully typed, even though legacy-lib.js has no types" }, "reference": { "label": "Declaration Files — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-files/introduction.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-017", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the danger of using a type assertion (`as SomeType`) instead of an actual type guard, and when is an assertion still legitimate to use?", "answer": "A type assertion tells the compiler \"trust me, treat this value as this type\" without performing any actual runtime check — it's purely a compile-time instruction with zero effect at runtime, so asserting an incorrect type produces no error at the assertion site; the mismatch only surfaces later, often confusingly, wherever the wrongly-typed value is actually used incorrectly.\n\nA legitimate use is when you genuinely have more specific knowledge than the type checker can infer on its own — e.g. `document.getElementById('root') as HTMLDivElement` when you know from the surrounding markup that the element is definitely a div, and the DOM API's necessarily generic `HTMLElement | null` return type can't express that. It's not legitimate as a shortcut past an actual type mismatch you haven't verified is safe — that's exactly the case a real type guard (a runtime check that actually validates the shape before narrowing) exists to handle correctly instead.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "const el = document.getElementById(\"root\") as HTMLDivElement; // legitimate — you know more than the DOM API can express\n\nconst value = externalApiResult as User; // risky — no runtime check, just asserted\n\nfunction isUser(x: unknown): x is User { // a real type guard, actually checks\n return typeof x === \"object\" && x !== null && \"id\" in x;\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Type Assertions — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#type-assertions" } }, { "id": "q-ts-018", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is an index signature in TypeScript, and what's the tradeoff of using one on an object type?", "answer": "An index signature (`{ [key: string]: number }`) declares that an object can have any number of properties, as long as every property's value matches the declared type — useful for representing a genuinely dynamic dictionary/map shape where the specific set of keys isn't known ahead of time (e.g. a lookup table keyed by an arbitrary user-supplied ID).\n\nThe tradeoff is that it weakens type safety for typos: accessing `obj.anyRandomKeyYouTypedWrong` still type-checks successfully (as the index signature's value type) even though that key was never actually intended to exist, since the index signature makes *any* string key valid by definition. For a genuinely fixed, known set of properties, an explicit interface (where accessing an undeclared property name is a compile error) is the safer and more precise choice; an index signature should be reserved for cases where the keys really are dynamic.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface ScoreBoard { [playerId: string]: number; } // dynamic keys\n\nconst scores: ScoreBoard = { alice: 10 };\nconsole.log(scores.blob); // compiles fine (type: number), even though \"blob\" was never set\n\ninterface FixedShape { id: string; name: string; }\n// const f: FixedShape = { id: \"1\" }; f.nmae; // compile error — real typo protection here" }, "reference": { "label": "Index Signatures — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#index-signatures" } }, { "id": "q-ts-019", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What do TypeScript decorators do, and what's a common real-world use case in a backend framework?", "answer": "A decorator is a function applied to a class, method, property, or parameter via `@decoratorName` syntax, which runs at definition time and can inspect or modify the thing it's attached to — commonly used to attach metadata (via `reflect-metadata`) that a framework reads later at runtime to drive behavior, rather than to change the decorated code's logic directly.\n\nA common real-world use case: NestJS uses decorators like `@Controller('/orders')` and `@Get(':id')` to attach routing metadata to a class and its methods declaratively — the actual routing logic lives in the framework, which reads this metadata via reflection at startup to wire up the real HTTP routes, letting the application code stay focused on declaring intent rather than manually registering routes imperatively.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "@Controller(\"/orders\")\nclass OrdersController {\n @Get(\":id\")\n getOrder(@Param(\"id\") id: string) {\n return { id }; // routing wired up by the framework reading this metadata at startup\n }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Decorators — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/decorators.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-020", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the practical effect of the `strict` compiler flag, and why do teams sometimes enable individual strict sub-flags gradually instead of all at once on an existing codebase?", "answer": "`strict: true` is a single umbrella flag that enables a whole family of stricter checks at once (`strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, and several others) — the recommended baseline for any new TypeScript project, since it catches meaningfully more bugs than the defaults.\n\nOn a large existing codebase originally written without strict mode, flipping the umbrella flag on all at once can surface hundreds or thousands of newly-flagged errors simultaneously, which is often impractical to fix in one pass — teams commonly enable the individual sub-flags one at a time (starting with the highest-value ones, like `strictNullChecks`), fixing the resulting errors for each flag before moving to the next, so the migration is incremental and reviewable rather than one enormous, risky change.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "// New project — enable everything at once\n// tsconfig.json: { \"compilerOptions\": { \"strict\": true } }\n\n// Large existing codebase — migrate incrementally\n// { \"compilerOptions\": { \"strictNullChecks\": true, \"noImplicitAny\": false } }\n// fix strictNullChecks errors, then flip noImplicitAny next, and so on" }, "reference": { "label": "TSConfig Reference — strict", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strict" } }, { "id": "q-ts-021", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the difference between the `node` and `classic`/`bundler` module resolution strategies in `tsconfig.json`, and why does this setting sometimes cause \"cannot find module\" errors that seem to contradict what actually runs at runtime?", "answer": "Module resolution controls how the compiler locates the file behind an import specifier — `node` resolution mimics Node.js's own algorithm (checking `node_modules`, resolving `package.json`'s `main`/`exports` fields, resolving directory imports to `index` files), while other strategies resolve differently and can disagree about whether a given import path is actually valid.\n\nA mismatch between the resolution strategy configured for the type checker and the one your actual bundler or runtime uses is exactly why an import can compile cleanly under TypeScript but fail at runtime, or vice versa — the type checker was reasoning about module resolution using different rules than whatever tool actually executes the code, which is why the `moduleResolution` setting should generally be chosen to match (or the newer `bundler` option chosen) whatever the real runtime/bundler actually does, not picked independently.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "// tsconfig.json\n{\n \"compilerOptions\": {\n \"moduleResolution\": \"bundler\", // match what your actual bundler/runtime does\n \"module\": \"ESNext\"\n }\n}\n// A mismatch here is exactly why \"tsc\" can compile clean while the app fails to import at runtime" }, "reference": { "label": "moduleResolution — TSConfig Reference", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#moduleResolution" } }, { "id": "q-ts-022", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is a generic constraint (``), and why would you add one instead of leaving a type parameter fully open?", "answer": "An unconstrained generic parameter (`function f(x: T)`) tells the compiler nothing about what `T` can do — you can't access any property or call any method on `x` inside the function body, since the compiler has to assume `T` could be absolutely anything, including a primitive with no members at all.\n\nA constraint (`function f(x: T)`) narrows what `T` is allowed to be to anything satisfying that shape, which lets the function body safely access `x.id` while still preserving the caller's more specific actual type through the generic (so calling it with a richer object still returns/preserves that richer type, rather than widening it down to just `{ id: string }`) — constraints let you have both: some guaranteed structure to work with inside the function, and full type preservation for the caller.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "function printId(x: T) { /* console.log(x.id); */ } // compile error — T could be anything\n\nfunction printId2(x: T): T {\n console.log(x.id); // safe — guaranteed by the constraint\n return x; // still returns the caller's richer specific type, not just { id: string }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Generic Constraints — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html#generic-constraints" } }, { "id": "q-ts-023", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is a template literal type, and what's a practical use for one beyond just concatenating string literal types?", "answer": "A template literal type (`` type Route = `/api/${string}` ``) applies the same interpolation syntax as a runtime template literal, but at the type level — producing a type representing the set of all strings matching that pattern, which the compiler can check string literal values against.\n\nA practical use is modeling a constrained set of valid event names or CSS-in-JS property combinations derived from other types — e.g. `` type ChangeEvent = `on${Capitalize}Change` `` mechanically derives `'onNameChange' | 'onAgeChange'` from a union `'name' | 'age'`, keeping event-name types automatically in sync with an underlying set of fields rather than requiring a separately hand-maintained list that can drift out of sync as fields are added or renamed.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "type Fields = \"name\" | \"age\";\ntype ChangeEvent = `on${Capitalize}Change`;\ntype Events = ChangeEvent; // \"onNameChange\" | \"onAgeChange\" — derived automatically\n\ntype Route = `/api/${string}`;\nconst valid: Route = \"/api/orders\"; // ok\n// const invalid: Route = \"/other\"; // compile error" }, "reference": { "label": "Template Literal Types — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-024", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the difference between an abstract class and an interface in TypeScript, given that TypeScript interfaces have no runtime representation at all?", "answer": "A TypeScript interface exists purely at compile time — it's fully erased during compilation, leaving no trace in the emitted JavaScript, and it can only declare a contract (member signatures), never provide actual implementation. An abstract class does compile to a real runtime construct (a real JS class, just one that can't be instantiated directly) and can mix abstract member declarations (which subclasses must implement) with concrete, shared implementation that subclasses inherit for free.\n\nChoose an interface when you only need to describe a shape/contract with zero runtime cost and no shared implementation to provide; choose an abstract class when related subclasses genuinely share real implementation logic you don't want duplicated across them — the same distinction that applies in fully compiled OOP languages, just with the added detail that TypeScript's interfaces carry literally zero runtime footprint at all, unlike a language where interfaces are a first-class runtime construct.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface Shape { area(): number; } // erased entirely — zero runtime trace\n\nabstract class ShapeBase {\n abstract area(): number;\n describe() { return `Area: ${this.area()}`; } // real shared implementation, inherited\n}\n\nclass Circle extends ShapeBase {\n constructor(private radius: number) { super(); }\n area() { return Math.PI * this.radius ** 2; }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Abstract Classes and Members — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/classes.html#abstract-classes-and-members" } }, { "id": "q-ts-025", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What does the `keyof` operator do, and how is it commonly combined with generics to write a type-safe property accessor function?", "answer": "`keyof T` produces a union type of all the property names (as string/number/symbol literal types) of `T` — for `{ id: string, name: string }`, `keyof T` is `'id' | 'name'`, a type representing exactly the valid keys of that specific object shape.\n\nCombined with a generic constraint, this is what makes a fully type-safe `getProperty` function possible: `function getProperty(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` only accepts a `key` argument that's actually a real property of the specific `obj` passed in, and its return type is inferred as exactly that property's type — passing a typo'd or nonexistent key name is a compile error, and the returned value's type is precise rather than a generic `any`, which a plain `(obj: any, key: string) => any` signature could never guarantee.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface User { id: string; name: string; }\ntype UserKey = keyof User; // \"id\" | \"name\"\n\nfunction getProperty(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {\n return obj[key];\n}\n\nconst user: User = { id: \"1\", name: \"Alice\" };\nconst name = getProperty(user, \"name\"); // string, inferred precisely\n// getProperty(user, \"nmae\"); // compile error — typo caught" }, "reference": { "label": "keyof Type Operator — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/keyof-types.html" } }, { "id": "q-ts-026", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What is variance in the context of TypeScript's structural type system, and why are method parameters checked \"bivariantly\" by default while function-type parameters are checked contravariantly?", "answer": "Variance describes how subtyping relationships between complex types (functions, generics) relate to the subtyping of their component types — contravariant parameter checking (the theoretically sound rule) means a function accepting a *more general* parameter type is a valid substitute for one accepting a more specific type, since it can handle everything the specific case would send it and more.\n\nTypeScript checks method syntax (`interface Animal { speak(sound: Dog): void }`) more permissively (\"bivariantly\") than standalone function-type properties (`interface Animal { speak: (sound: Dog) => void }`) for pragmatic, historical compatibility reasons with common JS patterns like array method callbacks — this inconsistency is a known, deliberate soundness tradeoff in TypeScript's type system, not a bug, and it's part of why TypeScript's type system is explicitly \"unsound\" in a few specific, well-documented spots rather than being a fully rigorous type theory implementation.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface Animal { speak(sound: Dog): void; } // method syntax — checked bivariantly\ninterface AnimalStrict { speak: (sound: Dog) => void; } // function property — checked contravariantly\n\nclass Dog { bark() {} }\nclass Puppy extends Dog { whine() {} }\n// Both styles compile differently strictly when substituting Dog <-> Puppy in \"speak\"" }, "reference": { "label": "Function Type Compatibility — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/type-compatibility.html#function-parameter-bivariance" } }, { "id": "q-ts-027", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What does `import type` do differently from a regular `import`, and why does it matter for build tooling?", "answer": "`import type { Foo } from './foo'` tells the compiler this import is used purely for type-checking purposes and should be completely erased from the emitted JavaScript — no runtime `require`/`import` statement for it will appear in the compiled output at all, unlike a regular import of a type, which the compiler can usually (but not always, especially with certain bundler/transpiler setups) figure out to elide on its own.\n\nThis matters most with build tools that transpile files one at a time in isolation (rather than type-checking the whole project first, as plain `tsc` does) — such a tool can't always tell whether an imported name is a type-only construct or an actual runtime value, and might either wrongly emit a genuine runtime import for a type that doesn't exist at runtime, or wrongly strip one that was actually needed; `import type` removes that ambiguity explicitly, which is why it's often required (via the `isolatedModules`/`verbatimModuleSyntax` flags) in projects using such tools.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "import type { User } from \"./types\"; // guaranteed erased — no runtime import emitted\nimport { fetchUser } from \"./api\"; // a real runtime import, kept\n\nfunction greet(user: User) { console.log(user.name); } // User only ever used as a type" }, "reference": { "label": "import type — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-8.html#type-only-imports-and-export" } }, { "id": "q-ts-028", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "Why doesn't TypeScript's type system provide any actual runtime safety, and what's the standard pattern for validating data at a genuine system boundary (an API response, form input, environment variables)?", "answer": "TypeScript types are fully erased during compilation — none of them exist at runtime in any form, so a type annotation is only ever a guarantee about what the *compiler believes* the shape of a value should be, based on the code paths it can statically analyze; it says nothing about data that enters the program from outside that analysis, like a parsed JSON response, `process.env`, or unvalidated form input, all of which TypeScript will happily let you assert an arbitrary type onto with zero actual runtime checking.\n\nThe standard pattern is to validate genuinely external data at the boundary using a runtime schema-validation library (Zod, Yup, io-ts) that both performs an actual runtime check and, as a bonus, can *derive* the corresponding TypeScript type from the same schema definition — so the compile-time type and the runtime validation logic can never silently drift out of sync with each other, which manually asserting a type onto unchecked external data would risk.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "import { z } from \"zod\";\n\nconst UserSchema = z.object({ id: z.string(), name: z.string() });\ntype User = z.infer; // derived from the same schema, can't drift\n\nconst parsed = UserSchema.parse(JSON.parse(rawApiResponse)); // throws if the shape is wrong" }, "reference": { "label": "Zod — schema validation", "url": "https://zod.dev/" } }, { "id": "q-ts-029", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the difference between the `target` and `module` compiler options in `tsconfig.json`, and why can setting them incorrectly for your deployment environment cause runtime failures that the compiler itself never warns about?", "answer": "`target` controls which JavaScript language version features the compiler downlevels newer syntax to (e.g. compiling optional chaining down to an equivalent `if` chain if targeting an older engine that doesn't support it natively) — set it too low for a modern runtime and you pay unnecessary transpilation overhead; set it too high and the emitted code uses syntax the actual runtime doesn't support, causing a runtime syntax error the compiler had no way to catch, since it isn't responsible for knowing what your actual deployment environment supports.\n\n`module` controls what module system the emitted code uses (CommonJS's `require`, or ES Modules' `import`) — mismatching this against how your runtime or bundler actually loads modules produces \"require is not defined\" or \"cannot use import statement outside a module\" errors that are purely a runtime/bundler-level mismatch, invisible to the type checker, since `tsc` type-checks and successfully emits its output regardless of whether the *target environment* would actually know what to do with that output.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "// tsconfig.json\n{\n \"compilerOptions\": {\n \"target\": \"ES2020\", // must match what your runtime actually supports\n \"module\": \"CommonJS\" // must match how your runtime loads modules (Node vs. bundler ESM)\n }\n}\n// tsc happily compiles regardless of whether the target runtime can execute the output" }, "reference": { "label": "target and module — TSConfig Reference", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#target" } }, { "id": "q-ts-030", "category": "TypeScript", "question": "What's the difference between `interface` extension (`interface A extends B`) and a type alias using an intersection (`type A = B & { ... }`) for combining shapes, and are they truly interchangeable?", "answer": "Both produce a type combining the members of multiple sources, and for simple, compatible object shapes they behave nearly identically. The meaningful difference shows up on conflict: `interface extends` requires that any overlapping property be compatible (assignable) between the base and the extension, and will raise a clear compile error immediately if they conflict incompatibly — an intersection type, on the other hand, will silently resolve a genuine property-type conflict (e.g. one source says `string`, another says `number`) down to the `never` type for that property, which is a much less obvious failure mode to diagnose, since the error only surfaces later wherever that now-`never` property is actually used.\n\nBecause of this, `interface extends` is generally the more forgiving choice specifically for straightforward object-shape composition where you want conflicts caught loudly and early, while intersections are more appropriate when combining genuinely independent, non-overlapping shapes where a silent `never` on an unexpected overlap is unlikely to occur in practice.", "snippet": { "language": "typescript", "code": "interface A { prop: string; }\ninterface B extends A { prop: number; } // compile error immediately — clear conflict\n\ntype A2 = { prop: string };\ntype B2 = A2 & { prop: number }; // compiles! prop becomes type 'never' — silent, surfaces later\nconst b: B2 = { prop: /* impossible to satisfy */ } as never;" }, "reference": { "label": "Interface Extension vs. Intersections — TypeScript Handbook", "url": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#interface-extension" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-003", "category": "System Design", "question": "What are the main load balancing algorithms, and what specific traffic pattern does each handle well or poorly?", "answer": "Round robin distributes requests evenly in rotation regardless of each backend's current load — simple, but poor when requests vary wildly in cost, since a backend handling several expensive requests in a row still gets the next one at its regular turn. Least-connections routes to whichever backend currently has the fewest active connections, adapting better to uneven request cost, but requires the load balancer to track live connection counts per backend.\n\nConsistent hashing routes based on a hash of some request attribute (a client ID, a cache key) so the same input consistently lands on the same backend — valuable for session affinity or maximizing cache hit rates on that backend, at the cost of potentially uneven load distribution if certain hash values are disproportionately popular (a hot key). The right choice depends on whether request cost is uniform, whether backend affinity matters, and whether the backend set changes size frequently (consistent hashing minimizes redistribution when nodes are added/removed, unlike naive modulo hashing).", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Round robin: req1->A, req2->B, req3->C, req4->A ... (ignores current load)\nLeast connections: route to whichever backend has the fewest active connections right now\nConsistent hashing: route(hash(clientId)) -> always the same backend for that client" }, "reference": { "label": "Load balancing algorithms — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/technology-choices/load-balancing-overview" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-004", "category": "System Design", "question": "What's the difference between cache-aside, write-through, and write-behind caching strategies?", "answer": "Cache-aside (lazy loading) has the application check the cache first on a read; on a miss, it reads from the database and populates the cache for next time. Writes typically just invalidate or update the cache entry directly. This is simple and only caches data that's actually requested, but leaves a brief window where a cache miss right after a write could read stale data if not handled carefully.\n\nWrite-through updates the cache and the database synchronously on every write, so the cache is never stale — at the cost of adding the cache-write latency to every write operation. Write-behind (write-back) updates the cache immediately but defers the database write to happen asynchronously, batched — fastest for the caller, but introduces a real risk of losing recently-written data if the cache fails before the deferred write completes, which is why it's reserved for data where that risk is acceptable in exchange for write throughput.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Cache-aside\nvar data = cache.Get(key) ?? await db.Load(key); cache.Set(key, data);\n\n// Write-through — cache and DB updated together, synchronously\ncache.Set(key, value); await db.Save(key, value);\n\n// Write-behind — cache updated now, DB write deferred/batched\ncache.Set(key, value); _writeBackQueue.Enqueue(key, value); // risk: lost if cache fails before flush" }, "reference": { "label": "Caching strategies — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-005", "category": "System Design", "question": "What makes cache invalidation genuinely hard, and what's the tradeoff between a short TTL and explicit invalidation on write?", "answer": "The core difficulty is that the cache and the source of truth are now two separate copies of the same data that can drift apart — any write path that updates the database but forgets to also update or invalidate the corresponding cache entry leaves stale data being served indefinitely, and as the number of write paths and cache keys grows, guaranteeing every single one correctly invalidates every relevant cache entry becomes genuinely error-prone.\n\nA short TTL bounds the maximum staleness window automatically without needing every write path to remember to invalidate anything, at the cost of the cache expiring (and needing a fresh database round-trip) even when the underlying data hasn't actually changed. Explicit invalidation on write eliminates unnecessary staleness entirely, but requires disciplined, comprehensive coverage of every code path that mutates the cached data — missing even one is a real, often hard-to-detect bug. Many systems combine both: explicit invalidation as the primary mechanism, with a TTL as a safety net against any invalidation path that was missed.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "cache.Set(key, value, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); // TTL: bounds staleness automatically\n\nasync Task UpdateOrder(Order order)\n{\n await db.SaveAsync(order);\n await cache.RemoveAsync($\"order:{order.Id}\"); // explicit invalidation: zero staleness, but easy to miss a path\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Cache invalidation strategies — AWS", "url": "https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-006", "category": "System Design", "question": "Compare the token bucket, leaky bucket, and sliding window algorithms for rate limiting.", "answer": "Token bucket maintains a bucket that refills with tokens at a steady rate up to a cap; each request consumes a token, and requests are rejected once the bucket is empty — this naturally allows short bursts up to the bucket's capacity while still enforcing a long-run average rate, which matches how real traffic often behaves (bursty, not perfectly smooth).\n\nLeaky bucket processes requests at a strictly constant output rate regardless of how bursty the input is (excess requests queue or are dropped), smoothing traffic out but adding latency to bursts rather than allowing them through immediately. Sliding window (log or counter-based) tracks request counts within a continuously moving time window rather than a fixed one, avoiding the boundary-burst problem of a naive fixed window (where a client could send double its allowed rate by timing requests just before and after a window reset) at the cost of needing more state to track the window precisely.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Token bucket: bucket has 10 tokens, refills 1/sec -> allows a burst of 10, then throttles to 1/sec\nLeaky bucket: requests queue, drain at a constant 1/sec regardless of burst size\nSliding window: count requests in the trailing 60s, not a fixed [0-60), [60-120) boundary" }, "reference": { "label": "Rate Limiting Strategies — Cloudflare", "url": "https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-007", "category": "System Design", "question": "What are the key components and design decisions in designing a URL shortener?", "answer": "The core problem is generating a compact, unique, non-colliding short code for each long URL and mapping between them — typically either by base-62 encoding an auto-incrementing ID (guaranteed unique, but reveals roughly how many URLs have been created and their creation order) or by hashing the URL and taking a prefix of the hash (needs a collision-check-and-retry step, but doesn't leak sequential information).\n\nBeyond the encoding scheme, the design has to account for read-heavy traffic (redirects vastly outnumber creations, so a cache in front of the datastore is essential), choosing between a 301 (permanent, cacheable by browsers, but analytics on click-through become harder since browsers may skip re-requesting) versus a 302 (temporary, always hits your server, easier to track click analytics) redirect, and a strategy for expiring or garbage-collecting unused short codes if the ID space is otherwise finite.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Base-62 encode an auto-incrementing ID\nstring ShortCode(long id) => ToBase62(id); // e.g. 125 -> \"cb\"\n\n// GET /{code} — 301 is cacheable by the browser; 302 always hits your server for click analytics\napp.MapGet(\"/{code}\", (string code) => Results.Redirect(urlStore[code], permanent: false));" }, "reference": { "label": "URL Shortener system design — Microsoft Learn (Azure architecture)", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/web-queue-worker" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-008", "category": "System Design", "question": "How would you design a scalable notification system that supports email, SMS, and push notifications?", "answer": "Decouple the act of *deciding* a notification should be sent from actually *delivering* it: application services publish a notification event (recipient, template, channel preference, payload) to a queue rather than calling a delivery provider directly and synchronously, so a slow or temporarily-down provider doesn't block or fail the originating request.\n\nA set of channel-specific worker consumers pull from that queue and handle the actual delivery per channel (each with its own provider integration, retry/backoff policy, and rate limits imposed by that provider), while a shared template/rendering layer keeps notification content consistent across channels. Track delivery status per notification (queued, sent, delivered, failed) so failures are visible and retriable, and support user-level preferences (opted out of SMS, quiet hours) as a filter applied before a notification is even queued for a given channel, rather than after the provider has already been called.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "await bus.PublishAsync(new NotificationRequested(userId, \"order-shipped\", channel: \"email\")); // decoupled from delivery\n\n// EmailWorker, SmsWorker, PushWorker each consume independently, own retry/backoff per provider\n// track: Queued -> Sent -> Delivered -> Failed, filtered by user preference before even queuing" }, "reference": { "label": "Notification system design — Microsoft Learn (Queue-Based Load Leveling)", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-009", "category": "System Design", "question": "How does a distributed unique ID generator like Twitter's Snowflake work, and what problem does it solve compared to a database auto-increment column?", "answer": "A database auto-increment ID guarantees uniqueness only within that single database instance — it doesn't work once you need multiple writers (sharded databases, multiple regions) generating IDs concurrently without coordinating on every single ID, since that coordination itself becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure at scale.\n\nSnowflake-style IDs are generated independently by each node with no coordination required per ID: each 64-bit ID packs a timestamp (making IDs roughly time-sortable), a fixed machine/worker ID (so different generators never produce colliding IDs even without talking to each other), and a per-millisecond sequence counter (handling multiple IDs requested within the same millisecond on the same machine). This gives globally unique, roughly sortable IDs generated locally at very high throughput, at the cost of IDs being larger than a simple integer and depending on reasonably synchronized clocks across machines.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "64-bit Snowflake ID:\n[ 41 bits: timestamp (ms) ][ 10 bits: machine/worker ID ][ 12 bits: per-ms sequence ]\n// Generated locally, no coordination needed, roughly time-sortable, globally unique" }, "reference": { "label": "Announcing Snowflake — Twitter Engineering", "url": "https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2010/announcing-snowflake" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-010", "category": "System Design", "question": "How does consistent hashing work, and what specific problem does it solve compared to simple modulo-based hashing when distributing keys across a set of cache nodes?", "answer": "With naive modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N` nodes), adding or removing even a single node changes the modulo divisor for nearly every key, causing almost the entire keyspace to remap to a different node all at once — a massive, unnecessary cache invalidation event every time the cluster resizes.\n\nConsistent hashing places both nodes and keys onto a conceptual ring (via hashing), and each key is owned by the next node found walking clockwise from the key's position on the ring. Adding or removing one node only affects the keys between it and its immediate neighbor on the ring — a small, bounded fraction of the total keyspace remaps, not nearly all of it — which is exactly why it's the standard approach for distributed caches and partitioned datastores that need to resize their node count without triggering a near-total cache/data reshuffle.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "hash(key) % N -- adding a node changes N -> nearly every key remaps\n\nConsistent hashing ring: nodes and keys both hashed onto a circle\n key owned by the next node clockwise -- adding/removing one node only remaps its neighboring slice" }, "reference": { "label": "Consistent Hashing — Microsoft Learn (Sharding pattern)", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-011", "category": "System Design", "question": "What role does a CDN play beyond just caching static assets, and how does it improve performance for dynamic content too?", "answer": "A CDN's core value is serving content from a point-of-presence physically closer to the requesting user than your origin server, cutting round-trip latency — most obviously valuable for static assets (images, JS/CSS bundles) that rarely change and can be cached at the edge for a long time with a versioned/hashed filename to invalidate safely on deploy.\n\nBeyond pure static caching, CDNs increasingly serve dynamic content acceleration too — terminating TLS at the edge (avoiding a full round trip to origin just for the handshake), routing requests over the CDN's own optimized backbone network back to origin rather than the public internet's often less direct path, and in some cases running edge compute (rewriting requests, serving personalized-but-cacheable variants) that reduces origin load even for content that isn't simply cacheable as-is.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Static: /app.a1b2c3.js served from the nearest edge PoP, cached for a year (hashed filename)\nDynamic: TLS terminated at the edge + CDN's optimized backbone back to origin (faster than public internet)\nEdge compute: rewrite/personalize a request before it even reaches origin" }, "reference": { "label": "What a CDN does — Microsoft Learn (Azure Front Door)", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/front-door-caching" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-012", "category": "System Design", "question": "What is the circuit breaker pattern, and what are its three states?", "answer": "A circuit breaker wraps calls to a potentially-failing dependency and tracks recent failure rates; once failures exceed a threshold, it \"trips\" and starts failing fast for a period — returning an immediate error (or a fallback) without even attempting the call — rather than letting every caller keep waiting on a slow, doomed request to a service that's already known to be down.\n\nIt has three states: Closed (normal operation, calls pass through and failures are counted), Open (tripped — calls fail immediately without attempting the real dependency, for a cooldown period), and Half-Open (after the cooldown, a limited number of test calls are allowed through to check if the dependency has recovered — success transitions back to Closed, failure trips it back to Open). This prevents a struggling downstream dependency from also exhausting the caller's own resources (threads, connections) waiting on calls that are very likely to fail or time out anyway.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "var breaker = Policy.Handle()\n .CircuitBreakerAsync(exceptionsAllowedBeforeBreaking: 5, durationOfBreak: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));\n// Closed -> failures accumulate -> Open (fails fast) -> after cooldown -> Half-Open (test calls) -> Closed or Open" }, "reference": { "label": "Circuit Breaker pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-013", "category": "System Design", "question": "What is the bulkhead pattern, and how does it prevent one failing dependency from taking down an entire service?", "answer": "Named after ship compartments that keep a hull breach in one section from flooding the whole vessel, the bulkhead pattern partitions resources (thread pools, connection pools) so that calls to different downstream dependencies each draw from their own isolated, capped pool rather than a single shared pool serving every dependency.\n\nWithout isolation, if one downstream dependency becomes slow, calls to it can consume every available thread/connection in a shared pool waiting on responses, starving completely unrelated requests to healthy dependencies of any resources at all — a single struggling dependency effectively takes down the whole service. With bulkheads, that same slow dependency can only exhaust its own dedicated, bounded pool; requests to other, healthy dependencies continue unaffected because they draw from a separate resource pool entirely.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "var paymentPool = new SemaphoreSlim(10); // dedicated bulkhead for the payment dependency\nvar searchPool = new SemaphoreSlim(20); // separate bulkhead for search — one can't starve the other\n\nawait paymentPool.WaitAsync();\ntry { await CallPaymentService(); } finally { paymentPool.Release(); }" }, "reference": { "label": "Bulkhead pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/bulkhead" } }, { "id": "q-sysdesign-014", "category": "System Design", "question": "What is backpressure in a streaming/event-driven system, and what happens if a system doesn't handle it?", "answer": "Backpressure is a mechanism for a slower consumer to signal to a faster producer that it needs to slow down — rather than the producer blindly continuing to push data at its own pace regardless of whether the consumer can actually keep up processing it.\n\nWithout backpressure, a producer that outpaces its consumer causes unbounded buffering somewhere in between (in memory, in a queue) as unconsumed data piles up faster than it drains — eventually exhausting memory, causing dropped messages, or cascading into failures elsewhere in the pipeline. Proper backpressure handling (bounded queues that block or reject new items once full, reactive streams' explicit demand-signaling protocols, or simply rate-limiting the producer based on consumer-reported capacity) keeps the whole pipeline's throughput bounded by its slowest stage instead of silently accumulating an ever-growing backlog.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "var channel = Channel.CreateBounded(capacity: 1000);
