"question": "How does combining retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers correctly prevent cascading failures, and what happens if you only implement one of the three?", "answer": "Timeouts alone bound how long any single call can hang, but without a circuit breaker a struggling downstream dependency still gets hit with a fresh full-timeout-duration attempt on every single subsequent request, needlessly consuming resources on calls very likely to fail or time out again anyway. Retries alone (without backoff or a circuit breaker) can actively make a struggling dependency worse by adding even more load exactly when it's least able to handle it, potentially turning a temporary slowdown into a full outage.\n\nUsed together correctly — a bounded timeout so no single call hangs indefinitely, a circuit breaker that stops sending traffic entirely once failures cross a threshold (giving the struggling dependency room to recover instead of piling on), and retries with backoff/jitter applied only to the calls that do go through — the combination prevents a single struggling dependency's slowness from consuming the calling service's own threads/connections and, transitively, cascading that slowness or failure up through everything that calls the calling service in turn.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "var policy = Policy.WrapAsync(\n Policy.Handle().WaitAndRetryAsync(3, i => TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Math.Pow(2, i))), // retry w/ backoff\n Policy.Handle().CircuitBreakerAsync(5, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)), // stop piling on\n Policy.TimeoutAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)) // bound each call\n);\n// Any one alone is insufficient: retries alone worsen an outage; timeout alone keeps re-attacking it" }, "reference": { "label": "Polly documentation", "url": "https://www.pollydocs.org/" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-018", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What's the difference between event notification and event-carried state transfer as styles of event-driven integration between services?", "answer": "Event notification publishes a lightweight event that essentially just says \"something happened\" (e.g. `OrderPlaced { orderId }`) without the full details — any consumer that needs more information has to call back to the publishing service's API to fetch it, keeping the event itself small but reintroducing a synchronous dependency on the publisher's availability at the moment a consumer actually processes the event.\n\nEvent-carried state transfer includes the relevant data directly in the event payload itself (`OrderPlaced { orderId, items, total, customerId }`), letting consumers act on the event using only the data it carries, with no callback to the publisher required — trading a larger, more duplicated event payload (and the need to think about schema evolution/backward compatibility for that payload over time) for genuine decoupling from the publisher's availability at consumption time. Many real systems use event-carried state transfer specifically to avoid the synchronous coupling that event notification's callback pattern reintroduces.", "snippet": { "language": "json", "code": "// Event notification — thin, requires a callback\n{ \"event\": \"OrderPlaced\", \"orderId\": 123 }\n\n// Event-carried state transfer — self-sufficient, no callback needed\n{ \"event\": \"OrderPlaced\", \"orderId\": 123, \"items\": [...], \"total\": 99.50, \"customerId\": 42 }" }, "reference": { "label": "Event-driven architecture styles — Martin Fowler", "url": "https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-019", "category": "Microservices", "question": "Why is designing an API contract-first (e.g. an OpenAPI spec written and agreed upon before implementation) valuable in a microservices team structure specifically?", "answer": "When the team building a service and the team(s) consuming it are different teams with independent schedules, waiting for the provider's implementation to be fully built before the consumer team can even start their own integration work serializes work that could otherwise happen in parallel — and it means any API design flaws are discovered only after real implementation effort has already gone into it on both sides.\n\nAgreeing on the API contract first (and generating server stubs/client SDKs from that same shared spec) lets both teams work in parallel against a mutually-agreed interface, catches design problems and mismatched expectations early — before either side has written real implementation code around a flawed contract — and the same spec doubles as living, always-accurate documentation and as the basis for contract testing later, rather than documentation drifting out of sync with an implementation that evolved ad hoc without ever updating a spec written for a separate purpose.", "snippet": { "language": "yaml", "code": "# orders-api.yaml — agreed before either team writes implementation code\npaths:\n /orders/{id}:\n get:\n responses:\n '200': { content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Order' } } } }\n# both teams generate stubs/clients from this and work in parallel" }, "reference": { "label": "OpenAPI Specification", "url": "https://swagger.io/specification/" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-020", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What is \"chatty\" service-to-service communication, and how does it typically get introduced during an initial monolith-to-microservices decomposition?", "answer": "Chatty communication is when accomplishing a single logical operation requires many separate network round trips between services (fetch the order, then separately fetch each line item's product details one at a time, then separately fetch the customer's shipping address) — each individual call might be fast, but the cumulative latency of many sequential round trips, plus the added failure surface of each one being a separate point of potential failure, adds up to real overall degradation.\n\nIt commonly gets introduced when a monolith is decomposed along boundaries drawn by mechanically extracting existing internal classes/modules into separate services without re-examining whether those objects were ever meant to be accessed together as one atomic unit — code that used to be several fast in-process method calls chained together becomes the same number of chained network calls, but each one now carries real network latency and failure risk that simply didn't exist when they were in-process calls within one process.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Chatty: 3 round trips for one logical operation\nvar order = await orderClient.GetAsync(id);\nvar product = await productClient.GetAsync(order.ProductId);\nvar address = await customerClient.GetAddressAsync(order.CustomerId);\n\n// Better: one aggregated call, or event-carried state avoiding the round trips entirely" }, "reference": { "label": "Chatty I/O antipattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/antipatterns/chatty-io/" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-021", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What's the tradeoff between sharing a common library across multiple microservices versus tolerating some code duplication between them?", "answer": "A shared library avoids duplicating genuinely identical logic (a common validation rule, a shared data model, standard error-handling conventions) across every service that needs it — but it also reintroduces a form of coupling: every service depending on that shared library now has to coordinate on its version, and a bug fix or breaking change in the shared library can ripple out and require redeploying every dependent service, working against the independent-deployability goal microservices were meant to provide.\n\nTolerating some duplication instead lets each service evolve its own copy of similar logic independently, with zero coupling between services through that logic — at the obvious cost of the same fix or improvement potentially needing to be made separately in multiple places, and a real risk of the duplicated copies gradually drifting apart in subtly inconsistent ways. The practical rule of thumb many teams use: share genuinely stable, rarely-changing, domain-agnostic infrastructure code (logging conventions, a common HTTP client wrapper) freely, but be much more cautious about sharing actual business logic across service boundaries, since that's exactly the kind of coupling most likely to reintroduce the tight coupling microservices are meant to avoid.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Share freely: a common HTTP client wrapper, logging conventions, error-response shape\nBe cautious: actual business rules (a shared \"OrderValidator\" couples every service to one version)\n// A bug fix in a shared business-logic library can force redeploying every dependent service" }, "reference": { "label": "Shared libraries in microservices — Chris Richardson", "url": "https://microservices.io/microservices/general/2019/07/09/soa-vs-microservice.html" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-022", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What's the difference between blue-green and canary deployment strategies for rolling out a new microservice version, and what does each optimize for?", "answer": "Blue-green deployment runs two complete, identical production environments (\"blue\" currently live, \"green\" the new version fully deployed but not yet receiving traffic), then switches all traffic over to green essentially instantaneously once it's verified healthy — giving a near-instant rollback (just switch traffic back to blue) if something's wrong, at the cost of needing double the infrastructure capacity running simultaneously during the transition.\n\nCanary deployment instead gradually shifts a small, increasing percentage of live traffic to the new version while most traffic still goes to the old one, closely monitoring the canary's actual error rates/latency on real traffic before continuing the rollout — this catches problems that only manifest under real production load/traffic patterns (which a fully-switched blue-green cutover wouldn't have caught in advance), at the cost of a slower rollout and the added complexity of running two versions simultaneously serving a split of live traffic for longer, with the associated need to handle any data/schema compatibility between the two versions during that overlap window.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Blue-green: blue (live) + green (new, fully deployed) both running -> flip 100% traffic at once\n rollback = flip back instantly, needs 2x capacity\n\nCanary: 95% traffic -> v1, 5% -> v2 -> monitor error rate -> gradually shift more if healthy\n catches real-traffic issues blue-green's instant cutover wouldn't" }, "reference": { "label": "Blue-green and canary deployments — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/aks/aks-cicd-github-actions-and-gitops#deployment-strategies" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-023", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What are the three pillars of observability (logs, metrics, traces), and why does having all three matter more than being excellent at just one?", "answer": "Logs give detailed, contextual records of discrete events (\"this specific request failed with this specific error\") — invaluable for deep debugging of one specific incident, but expensive to store at high volume and not well-suited to quickly answering \"how is the system doing overall right now.\" Metrics are aggregated numerical measurements over time (request rate, error rate, p99 latency) — cheap to store and great for dashboards, alerting, and spotting trends, but they can't tell you the specific story of any one individual failed request.\n\nTraces show the full path (and timing at each step) a single request took across multiple services — exactly what's needed to pinpoint *which* service in a chain introduced the latency or failure for a specific slow/failed request, something neither aggregated metrics nor an isolated log line from one service can show on its own. In practice, diagnosing a real production issue typically starts with metrics/alerting noticing something's wrong, traces narrowing down which specific service and request path is the problem, and logs providing the detailed context of exactly what happened there — each pillar answers a different question, and missing any one of them leaves a real gap in what you can diagnose.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Metrics: p99_latency{service=\"orders\"} = 850ms -- \"something's slow\" (alert fires)\nTraces: order request -> orders-svc (10ms) -> inventory-svc (820ms) -- \"inventory-svc is the culprit\"\nLogs: [inventory-svc] \"DB connection pool exhausted at 14:32:01\" -- the specific root cause" }, "reference": { "label": "Observability primer — OpenTelemetry docs", "url": "https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-024", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What are the key tradeoffs between choosing Kafka and RabbitMQ as the message broker for a microservices architecture?", "answer": "Kafka is built around a durable, append-only, partitioned log — messages are retained for a configured period (not deleted immediately on consumption) and multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream of events at their own pace, replaying from an earlier offset if needed; it's built for very high throughput and naturally fits event-sourcing/event-streaming use cases where the event history itself has ongoing value, not just momentary delivery.\n\nRabbitMQ is a more traditional message broker built around queues and flexible routing (direct, topic, fanout exchanges) — messages are typically consumed and removed, it supports more complex per-message routing logic and priority/delay features out of the box more naturally, and it's often simpler to reason about for straightforward task-queue/work-distribution use cases that don't need Kafka's log-retention/replay model. The choice generally comes down to whether you need Kafka's high-throughput event-log/replay semantics, or RabbitMQ's more flexible routing and simpler queue-based task distribution model.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Kafka: high-throughput log, retained + replayable, multiple consumer groups read independently\n consumer.subscribe([\"orders\"]); consumer.seek(partition, olderOffset); // replay from earlier\n\nRabbitMQ: flexible routing (direct/topic/fanout), messages typically consumed and removed\n channel.basicPublish(\"orders.exchange\", \"orders.created\", null, payload);" }, "reference": { "label": "Kafka vs RabbitMQ — Apache Kafka documentation", "url": "https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-025", "category": "Microservices", "question": "Why does schema evolution matter for event payloads in a microservices architecture, and what's the difference between backward-compatible and forward-compatible changes?", "answer": "Multiple independently-deployed consumers of the same event stream will inevitably be running different versions of their own code at any given moment — a producer can't simply change an event's schema and expect every consumer to have simultaneously updated to handle the new shape, since services deploy on their own independent schedules, not in lockstep.\n\nA backward-compatible change (adding a new optional field, for instance) means new events can still be correctly read by old consumer code that doesn't know about the new field — it just ignores it. A forward-compatible change means old events (already published before the schema changed) can still be correctly read by new consumer code — e.g. a new consumer needs to handle the case where an older event is missing a field that only started being populated later. Designing events to be both backward and forward compatible (avoiding removing or renaming fields, giving new fields sensible defaults, using a schema registry to enforce compatibility rules on every schema change) avoids a coordinated, all-at-once deployment across every producer and consumer every time an event's shape needs to evolve.", "snippet": { "language": "json", "code": "// v1\n{ \"orderId\": 123, \"total\": 99.50 }\n\n// v2 — backward compatible: old consumers ignore the new optional field\n{ \"orderId\": 123, \"total\": 99.50, \"currency\": \"USD\" }\n// forward compatible: new consumer code must handle older events missing \"currency\" gracefully" }, "reference": { "label": "Schema evolution and compatibility — Confluent docs", "url": "https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/schema-evolution.html" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-026", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What is the strangler fig pattern, and why is it generally preferred over a full rewrite when decomposing an existing monolith?", "answer": "A full rewrite requires building an entire replacement system before it can go live, deferring all value delivery until that (often optimistically estimated) completion date, freezing meaningful new feature work on the old system for the duration, and risking that the new system, built against requirements understood at the *start* of the rewrite, is already somewhat out of date with real business needs by the time it finally ships.\n\nThe strangler fig pattern instead incrementally routes specific pieces of functionality to new services standing alongside the existing monolith (via a routing layer/facade), migrating one capability at a time while the monolith continues handling everything not yet migrated — each migrated piece delivers value and gets validated against real production traffic immediately, feature work on both old and new pieces can continue in parallel throughout the migration, and if a particular decomposition turns out to be a poor fit partway through, the blast radius of that mistake is contained to just that one piece rather than an entire failed rewrite.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Routing facade sits in front of both:\n /checkout/* -> new CheckoutService (migrated)\n /* -> LegacyMonolith (everything not yet migrated)\n// Migrate one capability at a time; each one ships and is validated independently" }, "reference": { "label": "Strangler Fig pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/strangler-fig" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-027", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What's the difference between CQRS applied within a single service and CQRS applied across a distributed microservices architecture with separate read and write services?", "answer": "Within a single service, CQRS typically means separating the code paths for commands (writes, which go through the full domain model and its invariant checks) and queries (reads, which can bypass that model and read directly from a simpler, denormalized projection optimized for the specific read pattern needed) — but both still usually run within the same service and often the same database, just with cleanly separated code paths.\n\nApplied across a distributed architecture, the write side and read side can become genuinely separate services with separate datastores entirely — a write service processes commands and publishes events reflecting the resulting state changes, and one or more independent read-side services consume those events to build and maintain their own purpose-built, denormalized read models (potentially in a different database technology entirely, chosen for query performance rather than transactional correctness). This gives independent scaling of reads versus writes and lets each read model be shaped exactly for its own specific query pattern, at the cost of the read models being eventually (not immediately) consistent with the write side, since they update asynchronously as events propagate.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Single-service CQRS: same DB, separated code paths\npublic void Handle(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) { /* full domain model, writes to OrdersDb */ }\npublic OrderSummaryDto Handle(OrderSummaryQuery q) => _db.OrderSummaries.Single(o => o.Id == q.Id);\n\n// Distributed CQRS: separate services + datastores, connected by events\n// WriteService publishes OrderPlaced -> ReadService projects it into its own denormalized store" }, "reference": { "label": "CQRS pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-028", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What's a concrete symptom that a system has been decomposed into microservices prematurely, before the underlying domain boundaries were actually well understood?", "answer": "A telling symptom is that a large fraction of feature changes require coordinated deployments across multiple services simultaneously — if delivering one new feature routinely means several teams have to carefully sequence and coordinate releasing their respective services together, the services were split along boundaries that don't actually correspond to independent areas of change, and the system has taken on all of microservices' operational complexity (network calls, distributed debugging, multiple deployments to coordinate) without getting the actual payoff of independent deployability that was the whole point.\n\nAnother common symptom is excessively chatty synchronous communication between two or three services that are almost always deployed and changed together anyway — a strong signal those services were probably drawn along the wrong seam and might genuinely belong back together as one service (or should be recombined), rather than needing yet more resilience/observability tooling bolted on to paper over communication overhead between pieces that arguably shouldn't have been split apart in the first place.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "Symptom: shipping \"add a discount code\" requires coordinated deploys of\n OrdersService + PricingService + PromotionsService, every single time\n// -> these three probably belong together; the boundary was drawn along the wrong seam" }, "reference": { "label": "Microservices premium — Martin Fowler", "url": "https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MicroservicePremium.html" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-029", "category": "Microservices", "question": "What role does a service mesh play beyond what an API Gateway already provides, and why do some architectures use both together?", "answer": "An API Gateway sits at the edge of the system, handling north-south traffic — requests coming in from external clients to the system as a whole. A service mesh instead handles east-west traffic — the internal, service-to-service communication happening entirely within the system — providing uniform mTLS encryption between services, consistent retry/circuit-breaking policy, and detailed traffic metrics for every internal call, typically implemented via a sidecar proxy deployed alongside each service instance rather than at one single edge entry point.\n\nUsing both together is common precisely because they address genuinely different traffic patterns: the gateway is the single, purpose-built front door for external client requests (auth, rate limiting, routing to the right backend), while the mesh provides consistent security and resilience for the (often much larger volume of) internal calls happening between services after a request has already entered the system — neither one is really a substitute for what the other specifically handles.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "API Gateway: north-south -- external client -> system (auth, rate limiting, routing)\nService Mesh: east-west -- service -> service, internal (mTLS, retries, metrics via sidecars)\n// Used together: gateway is the front door, mesh secures everything happening after that" }, "reference": { "label": "Service mesh vs. API gateway — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/design/gateway#gateway-and-service-mesh" } }, { "id": "q-microservices-030", "category": "Microservices", "question": "When is microservices architecture explicitly the wrong choice, even though it's often presented as the modern default?", "answer": "For a small team (roughly, a handful of engineers) building a system without an urgent, proven need for independently scaling different components or for multiple teams to deploy independently, microservices mostly add operational overhead — network latency and failure modes where there used to be none, distributed debugging complexity, and the need to run and monitor many separate deployable units — without a corresponding organizational or scaling problem that overhead is actually solving.\n\nIt's also generally the wrong choice early in a genuinely new product's life, before the domain's real boundaries are well understood — splitting into services along guessed boundaries before you've learned (through actual usage and iteration) where the real seams in the domain actually lie tends to produce painfully wrong service boundaries that are far more expensive to correct once split apart (requiring cross-service data migration and API renegotiation) than they would have been to correct within a single, more malleable monolithic codebase. A well-structured, modular monolith — with clean internal boundaries that could later be extracted if and when an actual proven need arises — is frequently the more pragmatic starting point.", "reference": { "label": "Monolith First — Martin Fowler", "url": "https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MonolithFirst.html" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-001", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Builder pattern, and what problem does it solve that a constructor with many optional parameters doesn't handle well?", "answer": "A constructor with a large number of parameters — especially several optional ones — forces callers to either provide a long, error-prone list of positional arguments (easy to accidentally swap two parameters of the same type) or forces you to write an unwieldy combinatorial explosion of overloaded constructors to cover every combination of which optional parameters are actually supplied.\n\nA Builder instead exposes a fluent, step-by-step API (`.WithName(...).WithAddress(...).Build()`) where each method sets one specific piece of the object being constructed and returns the builder itself for chaining, only assembling the final immutable object once `.Build()` is called — this makes the construction call site self-documenting (each value is clearly labeled by the method name that sets it, not just position), lets optional parameters be omitted entirely with no overload explosion, and can validate the combination of provided values once, at the single `.Build()` call, rather than needing every possible constructor overload to separately re-validate its own particular combination of arguments.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public class PersonBuilder\n{\n private string _name = \"\";\n private int? _age;\n\n public PersonBuilder WithName(string name) { _name = name; return this; }\n public PersonBuilder WithAge(int age) { _age = age; return this; }\n public Person Build() => new Person(_name, _age);\n}\n\nvar person = new PersonBuilder().WithName(\"Alex\").WithAge(30).Build(); // self-documenting call site" }, "reference": { "label": "Builder pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/builder" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-002", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Facade pattern, and how does it differ from simply adding convenience methods to an existing class?", "answer": "A Facade introduces a new, simplified interface in front of a complex subsystem made up of multiple interacting classes — client code interacts only with the facade's simpler surface, without needing to understand or directly coordinate the subsystem's internal classes and their interactions at all, even though the facade doesn't remove or restrict access to those underlying classes for code that genuinely does need finer-grained control.\n\nThe distinction from convenience methods on an existing class: a facade is specifically about simplifying access to a *multi-class subsystem* the facade itself doesn't own the core logic of — it coordinates calls across several existing classes into one simpler entry point — rather than adding a shortcut method to a single class's own existing responsibilities. A common real example is a `VideoConverter` facade that internally coordinates a codec class, an audio mixer, and a file writer — client code just calls `converter.Convert(file, format)` without needing to understand or directly orchestrate those three collaborating pieces itself.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "class VideoConverterFacade\n{\n public File Convert(string filename, string format)\n {\n var codec = new CodecFactory().Extract(filename); // subsystem class 1\n var audio = new AudioMixer().Mix(filename); // subsystem class 2\n return new FileWriter().Write(codec, audio, format); // subsystem class 3\n }\n}\n\nvar converter = new VideoConverterFacade();\nconverter.Convert(\"movie.mp4\", \"avi\"); // caller never touches the 3 pieces above" }, "reference": { "label": "Facade pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/facade" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-003", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Proxy pattern, and what are the main variants (virtual, protection, remote) used for?", "answer": "A Proxy implements the same interface as a real subject object and controls access to it, sitting transparently between the client and the real object so the client interacts with the proxy exactly as if it were the real thing, unaware that extra behavior is happening around the actual call.\n\nA virtual proxy defers creating an expensive real object until it's actually needed (lazy initialization behind a stand-in that looks like the real thing from the outside). A protection proxy adds an access-control check before delegating to the real object, restricting who can actually invoke it based on the caller's permissions. A remote proxy represents an object that actually lives in a different process or on a different machine, hiding the networking/serialization details behind what looks like a normal, local method call to the client code. All three share the same shape — same interface, controlled delegation — applied to different specific concerns (cost, access, location).", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IReport { string Render(); }\nclass RealReport : IReport { public string Render() { /* expensive to build */ return \"...\"; } }\n\nclass LazyReportProxy : IReport // virtual proxy\n{\n private RealReport? _real;\n public string Render() => (_real ??= new RealReport()).Render(); // created only when needed\n}\n\nclass ProtectedReportProxy : IReport // protection proxy\n{\n private readonly IReport _real; private readonly bool _isAuthorized;\n public string Render() => _isAuthorized ? _real.Render() : throw new UnauthorizedAccessException();\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Proxy pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/proxy" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-004", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Command pattern, and what capability does it unlock (like undo/redo or a request queue) that calling a method directly doesn't?", "answer": "The Command pattern encapsulates a request — the action to perform, along with the specific parameters/receiver it needs — as an object of its own, implementing a common `Execute()` interface, rather than the caller invoking a method directly and immediately.\n\nBecause the request is now a first-class object rather than an immediate method call, it can be stored, queued, logged, passed around, and executed later or by something entirely decoupled from whoever originally created it — enabling patterns like undo/redo (each executed command object also implements an `Undo()` that reverses its specific effect, and a history stack of executed commands can be walked backward), a request queue (commands are enqueued and a worker executes them later, possibly on a different thread), or macro commands (a composite command that executes a sequence of other command objects as one logical unit) — none of which are naturally possible if the action is just an immediate, direct method call with no separate object representing it.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface ICommand { void Execute(); void Undo(); }\n\nclass AddTextCommand : ICommand\n{\n private readonly StringBuilder _doc; private readonly string _text;\n public AddTextCommand(StringBuilder doc, string text) { _doc = doc; _text = text; }\n public void Execute() => _doc.Append(_text);\n public void Undo() => _doc.Length -= _text.Length;\n}\n\nvar history = new Stack();\nvar cmd = new AddTextCommand(document, \"Hello\");\ncmd.Execute(); history.Push(cmd);\nhistory.Pop().Undo(); // undo the last executed command" }, "reference": { "label": "Command pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/command" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-005", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Template Method pattern, and how does it differ from the Strategy pattern given that both involve varying behavior in subclasses/implementations?", "answer": "Template Method defines the overall skeleton/sequence of an algorithm in a base class method, with certain individual steps deferred to abstract methods that subclasses override to provide their specific implementation of just those steps — the base class controls and fixes the overall structure and ordering, while subclasses only fill in specific, well-defined gaps within that fixed structure. It relies on inheritance: a subclass extends the base class and overrides selected steps.\n\nStrategy instead extracts the *entire* varying algorithm into a separate, swappable object implementing a common interface, injected into (composed with) the class that uses it — the algorithm can be swapped wholesale, at runtime, by handing in a different strategy object, rather than being fixed at compile time by which subclass was instantiated. The practical distinction: Template Method fits when the overall sequence of steps is genuinely fixed and shared, with only specific sub-steps varying (favor inheritance); Strategy fits when the entire algorithm needs to be swappable as a whole unit, potentially at runtime (favor composition) — which also makes Strategy the more flexible, more testable choice in most modern codebases that generally favor composition over inheritance.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Template Method: fixed skeleton, subclasses fill in steps\nabstract class ReportGenerator\n{\n public void Generate() { var data = FetchData(); Console.WriteLine(Format(data)); } // fixed sequence\n protected abstract string FetchData();\n protected abstract string Format(string data);\n}\n\n// Strategy: whole algorithm swapped in from outside\ninterface IFormatter { string Format(string data); }\nclass ReportGeneratorV2 { public ReportGeneratorV2(IFormatter formatter) { /* swappable at runtime */ } }" }, "reference": { "label": "Template Method pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/template-method" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-006", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Chain of Responsibility pattern, and what's a concrete real-world use case for it?", "answer": "Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of potential handler objects, each of which decides either to handle the request itself, pass it along to the next handler in the chain, or both — the sender of the request doesn't need to know in advance which specific handler in the chain will actually end up processing it, only that the request will be given the opportunity to be handled somewhere along the chain.\n\nA concrete, familiar real-world use case is exactly the middleware pipeline pattern found in most modern web frameworks (ASP.NET Core, Express) — each middleware component gets a chance to inspect/handle the incoming request and decides whether to pass it further down the chain to the next component, without the request's originator (the web server receiving the raw connection) needing to know anything about which specific middleware will ultimately process a given request; another classic example is a support ticket escalation system, where a ticket is passed up through tiers of support staff until one with sufficient authority/expertise actually handles it.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "abstract class SupportHandler\n{\n protected SupportHandler? Next;\n public SupportHandler SetNext(SupportHandler next) { Next = next; return next; }\n public abstract void Handle(Ticket ticket);\n}\n\nclass Tier1Handler : SupportHandler\n{\n public override void Handle(Ticket ticket)\n {\n if (ticket.Severity <= 1) Console.WriteLine(\"Tier 1 resolved it\");\n else Next?.Handle(ticket); // passed further down the chain\n }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Chain of Responsibility pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/chain-of-responsibility" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-007", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Mediator pattern, and what specific coupling problem does it solve among a group of interacting objects?", "answer": "Without a mediator, a group of objects that need to interact with each other directly (a set of UI form controls that need to enable/disable/update each other based on each other's state) each end up holding direct references to every other object they need to communicate with — as the number of interacting objects grows, the number of direct pairwise relationships between them grows much faster, producing a tangled web of interdependencies that's hard to reason about or modify without touching many objects at once.\n\nA Mediator centralizes that communication logic into one separate object — each participant object only needs a reference to the mediator, not to every other participant directly, and notifies the mediator of its own state changes; the mediator then decides what, if anything, needs to happen to the other participants as a result. This collapses many-to-many direct object coupling into many-to-one coupling through the mediator, at the cost of the mediator itself potentially becoming a large, complex class if the interaction logic it centralizes is itself genuinely complex.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IDialogMediator { void Notify(object sender, string ev); }\n\nclass LoginDialog : IDialogMediator\n{\n private Checkbox _rememberMe = new(); private TextBox _username = new();\n public void Notify(object sender, string ev)\n {\n if (sender == _rememberMe && ev == \"checked\")\n _username.Enabled = true; // mediator decides the effect, not the checkbox itself\n }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Mediator pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/mediator" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-008", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Memento pattern, and how does it capture and restore an object's state without violating its encapsulation?", "answer": "The Memento pattern lets an object (the \"originator\") produce a snapshot of its own internal state, packaged as an opaque memento object that external code (a \"caretaker,\" like an undo-history manager) can store and later hand back to the originator to restore that earlier state — but the caretaker holding onto the memento is never allowed to inspect or modify its contents itself; it can only store it and pass it back.\n\nThis preserves encapsulation because only the originator itself knows how to construct a memento from its own internals and how to interpret one to restore its state — a memento's internal structure is essentially private to the originator class, and outside code (the caretaker) treats it purely as an opaque token to be stored and later returned, never reaching in and directly manipulating the originator's internal fields the way a naive \"just expose all internal state publicly to allow saving/restoring it\" approach would require.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "class EditorMemento { public string Content { get; } internal EditorMemento(string c) => Content = c; }\n\nclass Editor\n{\n public string Text = \"\";\n public EditorMemento Save() => new EditorMemento(Text); // originator builds the snapshot\n public void Restore(EditorMemento m) => Text = m.Content; // and interprets it back\n}\n\nvar history = new Stack(); // caretaker: stores it, never inspects it\nhistory.Push(editor.Save());\neditor.Restore(history.Pop());" }, "reference": { "label": "Memento pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/memento" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-009", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Visitor pattern, and what specific problem with adding new operations to a class hierarchy does it solve?", "answer": "Given a class hierarchy of related types (different node types in an AST, different shape types), adding a new operation that needs different behavior per concrete type normally means adding a new virtual method to the base class and overriding it in every single subclass — fine for a stable hierarchy, but it means every new operation requires touching and redeploying every class in the hierarchy, which is awkward when the hierarchy is owned by a different team/library or the operations vary and grow far more often than the type hierarchy itself does.\n\nVisitor inverts this: each element in the hierarchy implements a single `Accept(visitor)` method that calls back into the appropriate typed `Visit` method on the visitor object (via double dispatch), and a *new operation* is added by writing an entirely new Visitor class implementing all the type-specific `Visit` methods for that one operation — adding a new operation touches zero existing element classes at all. The tradeoff is the reverse: adding a genuinely *new element type* to the hierarchy now requires updating every existing Visitor implementation to handle it, so Visitor fits best when the type hierarchy is comparatively stable but the set of operations performed over it grows and changes frequently.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IShapeVisitor { void Visit(Circle c); void Visit(Square s); }\ninterface IShape { void Accept(IShapeVisitor visitor); }\n\nclass Circle : IShape { public void Accept(IShapeVisitor v) => v.Visit(this); } // dispatch #1\nclass Square : IShape { public void Accept(IShapeVisitor v) => v.Visit(this); }\n\nclass AreaVisitor : IShapeVisitor // new operation — zero changes to Circle/Square\n{\n public void Visit(Circle c) => Console.WriteLine(\"circle area\");\n public void Visit(Square s) => Console.WriteLine(\"square area\");\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Visitor pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/visitor" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-010", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Composite pattern, and how does it let client code treat an individual object and a group of objects through the same interface?", "answer": "Composite defines a common interface shared by both individual (\"leaf\") objects and \"composite\" objects that themselves contain a collection of other objects implementing that same interface — a composite's own implementation of each interface method typically just delegates the call to each of its children in turn, recursively, so an operation invoked on the top-level composite naturally propagates down through the entire tree structure.\n\nThis lets client code treat a single leaf object and an arbitrarily deep tree of nested composites completely uniformly through the same interface, with no need for `if (isLeaf) ... else ...` branching logic scattered throughout client code — a classic example is a file system, where both a `File` (leaf) and a `Folder` (composite, containing files and other folders) implement a common `GetSize()` method; calling it on a top-level folder naturally recurses through the whole tree without the calling code needing to know or care about the actual depth or shape of that tree at all.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IFileSystemEntry { long GetSize(); }\n\nclass File : IFileSystemEntry { private long _size; public long GetSize() => _size; }\n\nclass Folder : IFileSystemEntry // composite\n{\n private readonly List _children = new();\n public long GetSize() => _children.Sum(c => c.GetSize()); // recurses through the whole tree\n}\n\nIFileSystemEntry root = new Folder();\nroot.GetSize(); // works identically whether root is a File or a deeply nested Folder" }, "reference": { "label": "Composite pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/composite" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-011", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Bridge pattern, and how does it differ from simple inheritance-based abstraction when you have two independently varying dimensions of behavior?", "answer": "If a class hierarchy needs to vary along two genuinely independent dimensions at once (say, different shape types *and* different rendering engines), representing that with plain inheritance alone forces a combinatorial explosion of subclasses covering every combination — `CircleOpenGL`, `CircleDirectX`, `SquareOpenGL`, `SquareDirectX`, and so on, growing multiplicatively as either dimension grows.\n\nBridge separates the two dimensions into two independent class hierarchies connected by composition rather than inheritance — an abstraction hierarchy (Shape, with subclasses Circle/Square) holds a reference to an implementor interface (Renderer, with implementations RendererOpenGL/RendererDirectX) and delegates the actual rendering work to whichever renderer implementation it's been given, rather than each shape subclass baking in one specific rendering approach directly. Either dimension can now grow independently — adding a new shape type or a new rendering engine each requires only one new class, not a new class for every existing combination with the other dimension.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IRenderer { void RenderCircle(float radius); }\nclass OpenGlRenderer : IRenderer { public void RenderCircle(float r) { /* ... */ } }\nclass DirectXRenderer : IRenderer { public void RenderCircle(float r) { /* ... */ } }\n\nabstract class Shape\n{\n protected readonly IRenderer Renderer; // bridge to the implementor hierarchy\n protected Shape(IRenderer renderer) => Renderer = renderer;\n public abstract void Draw();\n}\n\nclass Circle : Shape { public Circle(IRenderer r) : base(r) { } public override void Draw() => Renderer.RenderCircle(5); }\n// New shape or new renderer = one new class, not a combination of every pair" }, "reference": { "label": "Bridge pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/bridge" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-012", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Flyweight pattern, and what specific memory problem does it solve by sharing object instances?", "answer": "When a program needs to represent an enormous number of similar objects (individual characters in a text editor, individual trees in a forest-rendering scene), instantiating a full, independent object per occurrence — each carrying its own copy of data that's actually identical across many occurrences (a character's font/glyph shape, a tree species' mesh/texture) — wastes a large amount of memory on redundant, duplicated data.\n\nFlyweight splits each object's data into intrinsic state (the part that's genuinely shared and identical across many occurrences — the glyph shape for the letter 'a', a tree species' visual mesh) and extrinsic state (the part that's unique per occurrence and must be supplied by the calling context at use time — the position and color of this specific instance on screen). A shared flyweight factory ensures only one actual object exists per distinct intrinsic-state combination, reused across every occurrence that shares it, while the caller supplies the small amount of per-occurrence extrinsic state separately each time it's actually used — dramatically cutting memory use for scenarios with massive numbers of largely-identical objects.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "class TreeType { public string Mesh = \"\"; public string Texture = \"\"; } // intrinsic, shared\n\nstatic class TreeFactory\n{\n private static readonly Dictionary _cache = new();\n public static TreeType Get(string species) =>\n _cache.TryGetValue(species, out var t) ? t : _cache[species] = new TreeType { Mesh = species };\n}\n\nclass Tree { public int X, Y; public TreeType Type; } // extrinsic (position) supplied per instance" }, "reference": { "label": "Flyweight pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/flyweight" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-013", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the State pattern, and how does it replace a large conditional (`if`/`switch` on a status field) with polymorphism?", "answer": "A naive implementation of an object whose behavior depends on its current status (an order that's Pending, Shipped, Delivered, or Cancelled, each allowing different operations) often ends up with every method riddled with `switch (status) { case Pending: ...; case Shipped: ...; }` branches scattered throughout the class, which grows unwieldy and error-prone to modify correctly as more states or operations are added.\n\nThe State pattern instead extracts each state into its own class implementing a common state interface, and the context object (the Order) delegates its behavior to whichever concrete state object it currently holds a reference to — transitioning state means simply swapping which state object the context holds, and each state class's own implementation of the relevant methods (`Ship()`, `Cancel()`) contains only the logic actually valid for that specific state, with no giant conditional anywhere. This is conceptually very close to the Strategy pattern structurally — the key difference is that State objects are explicitly expected to trigger transitions to other states as part of normal operation, whereas a Strategy is typically chosen once by external code and doesn't switch itself out on its own.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IOrderState { void Ship(OrderContext ctx); }\nclass Pending : IOrderState { public void Ship(OrderContext ctx) => ctx.State = new Shipped(); }\nclass Shipped : IOrderState { public void Ship(OrderContext ctx) => throw new InvalidOperationException(\"Already shipped\"); }\n\nclass OrderContext\n{\n public IOrderState State = new Pending();\n public void Ship() => State.Ship(this); // no switch statement anywhere\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "State pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/state" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-014", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Iterator pattern, and why does most modern language tooling (`foreach`, `for...of`) mean developers rarely implement it manually anymore?", "answer": "Iterator provides a standard way to traverse the elements of a collection sequentially, without exposing that collection's underlying internal representation (an array, a linked list, a tree) to the code doing the traversal — client code interacts only through a common `HasNext()`/`Next()`-style interface, entirely decoupled from how the collection actually stores its elements internally.\n\nModern languages bake this pattern directly into first-class language syntax — C#'s `IEnumerable`/`yield return` and `foreach`, JavaScript's iterator protocol and `for...of` — so developers get the pattern's benefit (uniform, encapsulated traversal regardless of the underlying collection's actual internal structure) essentially for free through built-in language constructs, rather than needing to hand-implement a custom iterator class and its interface manually the way you would in an older language lacking this native support, which is exactly why Iterator is one of the classic design patterns developers apply constantly in practice without necessarily thinking of it by that name.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "class NumberRange : IEnumerable\n{\n private readonly int _start, _end;\n public NumberRange(int start, int end) { _start = start; _end = end; }\n public IEnumerator GetEnumerator() { for (int i = _start; i <= _end; i++) yield return i; }\n IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => GetEnumerator();\n}\n\nforeach (var n in new NumberRange(1, 5)) Console.WriteLine(n); // Iterator, for free via foreach" }, "reference": { "label": "Iterators — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/iterators" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-015", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Prototype pattern, and when is cloning an existing object actually preferable to constructing a new one from scratch?", "answer": "Prototype creates new objects by copying (cloning) an existing, already-configured instance rather than constructing a fresh one via its constructor and then separately configuring it step by step — the source object exposes a `Clone()` method that knows how to produce an independent copy of itself, including correctly handling whether nested objects need a deep or shallow copy.\n\nIt's preferable when constructing an object from scratch is genuinely expensive (an object that required significant setup, computation, or an expensive resource acquisition to reach its current configured state) and you need many similar-but-not-identical instances derived from that same expensive baseline — cloning an already-configured prototype and then tweaking just the specific differing fields is cheaper than repeating that full expensive construction process from scratch for every new instance. It's also useful when the exact concrete type of object to create isn't known statically at compile time but an existing instance of the right type is already available to clone from.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "class EnemyTemplate : ICloneable\n{\n public string Name = \"\"; public int[] StatsBlock = new int[50]; // expensive to build\n public object Clone() => new EnemyTemplate { Name = Name, StatsBlock = (int[])StatsBlock.Clone() };\n}\n\nvar baseGoblin = new EnemyTemplate { Name = \"Goblin\" };\nvar goblin2 = (EnemyTemplate)baseGoblin.Clone();\ngoblin2.Name = \"Goblin Archer\"; // cheaper than rebuilding StatsBlock from scratch" }, "reference": { "label": "Prototype pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/prototype" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-016", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Repository pattern, and what specific concern does it decouple the rest of an application's business logic from?", "answer": "A Repository provides a collection-like interface (`GetById`, `Add`, `FindByStatus`) for accessing and persisting domain objects, hiding the actual data access technology (raw SQL, an ORM like EF Core, a call to an external API) entirely behind that interface — application/business logic depends only on the repository's abstract interface, never on the concrete persistence mechanism underneath it.\n\nThis decouples business logic from data-access technology specifically: the persistence mechanism can be swapped (a different database, a different ORM) or mocked out entirely for unit testing business logic in isolation, without touching any of the code that actually uses the repository's interface — as long as the new implementation still satisfies the same abstract contract. The Dependency Inversion Principle is effectively what's being applied here: business logic defines the repository interface it needs, and the concrete data-access implementation depends on and implements that interface, rather than business logic depending directly on a concrete data-access class.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public interface IOrderRepository\n{\n Order? GetById(int id);\n void Add(Order order);\n}\n\npublic class EfOrderRepository : IOrderRepository // hides EF Core behind the interface\n{\n private readonly AppDbContext _db;\n public EfOrderRepository(AppDbContext db) => _db = db;\n public Order? GetById(int id) => _db.Orders.Find(id);\n public void Add(Order order) => _db.Orders.Add(order);\n}\n// Business logic depends only on IOrderRepository — swappable, mockable" }, "reference": { "label": "Repository pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/infrastructure-persistence-layer-design" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-017", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Unit of Work pattern, and how does it complement the Repository pattern rather than duplicate it?", "answer": "Repository handles *how* individual domain objects are fetched and persisted; Unit of Work tracks the set of changes made across potentially multiple repositories during a single logical business operation, and commits (or rolls back) all of them together as one atomic transaction — it answers \"when and how do all these related changes get saved together,\" not \"how does any one entity type get saved.\"\n\nWithout a Unit of Work, a business operation touching multiple entities (updating an Order and separately decrementing Inventory) that each call their own repository's `Save()` independently risks a partial failure — one succeeds and commits while the other fails, leaving the two related changes inconsistent with each other. Unit of Work coordinates all the changes made across the operation and wraps them in a single transaction boundary, so either all of them commit together or none do — EF Core's `DbContext`, for instance, already largely functions as a built-in Unit of Work (tracking changes across multiple entity types and committing them together on a single `SaveChanges()` call), which is exactly why layering an additional, explicit Unit of Work abstraction on top of it is sometimes considered redundant over-abstraction rather than genuinely necessary.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public class PlaceOrderService\n{\n private readonly AppDbContext _context; // acts as the Unit of Work\n\n public void PlaceOrder(Order order, InventoryUpdate update)\n {\n _context.Orders.Add(order);\n _context.InventoryUpdates.Add(update);\n _context.SaveChanges(); // both commit together, or neither does\n }\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Unit of Work pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/infrastructure-persistence-layer-design#the-repository-and-unit-of-work-patterns" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-018", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Specification pattern, and what problem does it solve compared to scattering the same business rule/query condition across multiple places in the codebase?", "answer": "The Specification pattern encapsulates a single business rule or query predicate (\"is this order eligible for expedited shipping,\" \"is this customer considered high-value\") as its own reusable object implementing a common `IsSatisfiedBy(candidate)` interface, rather than that same conditional logic being copy-pasted inline (as an `if` statement, or a LINQ `.Where()` clause) wherever it happens to be needed across the codebase.\n\nThis solves the specific problem of rule logic drifting out of sync with itself over time — if \"high-value customer\" is defined by a scattered set of independently-written conditionals in five different places, updating the actual business definition means finding and correctly updating all five (easy to miss one, producing inconsistent behavior); with a single Specification object, every place that needs that rule references the same one definition, and specifications can also be composed together (AND/OR/NOT combinations of specifications) to build more complex rules out of simpler, independently-reusable and independently-testable pieces.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public interface ISpecification { bool IsSatisfiedBy(T candidate); }\n\npublic class HighValueCustomerSpec : ISpecification\n{\n public bool IsSatisfiedBy(Customer c) => c.LifetimeValue > 10000; // one definition, everywhere\n}\n\nvar spec = new HighValueCustomerSpec();\nvar vips = customers.Where(spec.IsSatisfiedBy).ToList();" }, "reference": { "label": "Specification pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/specification" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-019", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "How does CQRS function as a design pattern at the class/module level within a single service, distinct from the broader system-level architectural style of the same name?", "answer": "At the class/module level, CQRS as a pattern is really just a discipline about separating the code path (and often the data models) used for commands (operations that change state, validated and processed through the domain model, typically returning little or nothing) from the code path used for queries (operations that read state, which can bypass the domain model entirely and read directly from whatever shape of data structure best serves that specific query, since a query has no need to enforce write-side invariants).\n\nThis is a narrower, more tactical application of the same underlying idea behind the full distributed system-level CQRS architecture (separate read/write services, separate datastores, eventual consistency between them) — within a single service, it's simply about not forcing both reads and writes through the exact same model and code path just because they happen to touch the same underlying entity, even when both still ultimately hit the same database. It can be adopted incrementally (separate command/query methods, or separate handler classes per command/query) without needing to commit to the much larger architectural complexity of the full distributed version.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public record PlaceOrderCommand(int CustomerId, List ItemIds);\npublic class PlaceOrderHandler { public void Handle(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) { /* writes through domain model */ } }\n\npublic record OrderSummaryQuery(int OrderId);\npublic class OrderSummaryHandler\n{\n public OrderSummaryDto Handle(OrderSummaryQuery q) =>\n _db.OrderSummaries.Single(o => o.OrderId == q.OrderId); // reads a shape suited to the query\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "CQRS pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-020", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Null Object pattern, and how does it eliminate a class of null-check-related bugs compared to returning or passing an actual `null` reference?", "answer": "Rather than a method returning an actual `null` reference to represent \"no result\" or \"nothing here\" (which then requires every caller to remember to explicitly check for null before using the result, or risk a null reference exception), the Null Object pattern returns a special object implementing the same interface as a real result, but with behavior that does nothing (or returns sensible, harmless defaults) instead of representing an absence that must be separately checked for.\n\nThis eliminates an entire category of bugs from a forgotten null check, since calling code can simply call methods on the returned object exactly as it would on a real one — a `NullLogger` implementation of an `ILogger` interface, for instance, silently discards every log call instead of the caller needing an `if (logger != null)` guard before every single logging call throughout the codebase. It's not universally appropriate (sometimes \"absence\" genuinely needs to be distinguished and handled differently from \"present but does nothing\"), but it's a clean fit for optional collaborators where doing nothing really is the correct behavior for the missing case.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public interface ILogger { void Log(string message); }\npublic class ConsoleLogger : ILogger { public void Log(string m) => Console.WriteLine(m); }\npublic class NullLogger : ILogger { public void Log(string m) { /* does nothing */ } }\n\nILogger logger = config.LoggingEnabled ? new ConsoleLogger() : new NullLogger();\nlogger.Log(\"Starting up\"); // no \"if (logger != null)\" needed anywhere" }, "reference": { "label": "Null Object pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/null-object" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-021", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What's the difference between using a DI container and \"pure DI\" (manually wiring dependencies via constructors with no container at all), and when might a team deliberately choose pure DI?", "answer": "A DI container resolves an object graph automatically at runtime based on registered type mappings and lifetimes — convenient at scale, since you don't manually wire up every single object's dependencies by hand as the object graph grows large and deeply nested, and lifetime management (singleton, scoped, transient) is handled centrally and consistently by the container.\n\nPure DI constructs the entire object graph manually and explicitly, typically in one composition root (`new OrderService(new OrderRepository(connectionString), new EmailNotifier(smtpConfig))`), with no reflection-based container involved at all — some teams deliberately choose this specifically because it's fully visible, debuggable, and compiler-checked (a missing dependency is a compile error, not a runtime \"unable to resolve\" exception discovered only when that code path actually executes), and it avoids the container becoming a kind of implicit, hard-to-trace \"magic\" that obscures the actual dependency graph. It tends to become unwieldy for very large, deeply-nested object graphs, which is exactly the case where a container's automation earns back its cost.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// DI container — resolved automatically at runtime\nbuilder.Services.AddScoped();\nbuilder.Services.AddScoped();\n\n// Pure DI — one explicit composition root, compiler-checked\nvar repository = new SqlOrderRepository(connectionString);\nvar orderService = new OrderService(repository, new EmailNotifier(smtpConfig));" }, "reference": { "label": "Dependency injection guidelines — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-022", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Object Pool pattern, and why is it applied selectively rather than as a default optimization for every object type?", "answer": "Object Pool maintains a pre-allocated set of reusable objects that are expensive to create or destroy (a database connection, a thread, a large buffer) — rather than constructing and discarding a fresh instance for every single use, code checks out an existing object from the pool, uses it, and returns it to the pool when finished, where it becomes available for reuse by the next caller instead of being garbage collected and eventually reallocated from scratch.\n\nIt's applied selectively because pooling adds real complexity — the pool itself needs thread-safe checkout/return logic, objects must be properly reset to a clean state before being handed to the next caller (a subtle and easy-to-get-wrong source of bugs, since state accidentally leaking between uses of a \"reset\" pooled object is a classic pooling pitfall), and for genuinely cheap-to-create objects, the pool's own bookkeeping overhead can exceed the cost of simply creating a fresh instance each time — pooling only pays off when the underlying object's creation/destruction cost is genuinely significant relative to the overhead of managing the pool itself.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "public class ConnectionPool\n{\n private readonly ConcurrentBag _pool = new();\n\n public DbConnection Rent() => _pool.TryTake(out var conn) ? conn : new DbConnection();\n public void Return(DbConnection conn) { conn.Reset(); _pool.Add(conn); } // must reset state first\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "ObjectPool in .NET — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/performance/objectpool" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-023", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What's the difference between the Factory Method and Abstract Factory patterns, given that both are commonly grouped together as \"factory patterns\"?", "answer": "Factory Method defines a single method (often overridden by subclasses) responsible for creating one specific kind of product — a base class defers the decision of exactly which concrete product class to instantiate to its subclasses, each subclass overriding the factory method to return its own specific product type, while the surrounding logic that uses the created product stays the same across all subclasses.\n\nAbstract Factory goes a level further, defining an interface for creating an entire *family* of related products that are meant to be used together (e.g. a UI toolkit's `CreateButton()`, `CreateCheckbox()`, and `CreateScrollbar()` all defined on one factory interface, with a concrete `WindowsFactory` and `MacFactory` each producing an internally-consistent, platform-appropriate set of all three) — the key distinction is that Abstract Factory groups multiple related creation methods together specifically to guarantee the resulting objects are mutually compatible with each other as a coherent family, which a single, standalone Factory Method has no mechanism to guarantee on its own.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Factory Method: one product per subclass\nabstract class DialogBase { public abstract IButton CreateButton(); }\nclass WindowsDialog : DialogBase { public override IButton CreateButton() => new WindowsButton(); }\n\n// Abstract Factory: a whole family of compatible products\ninterface IUiFactory { IButton CreateButton(); ICheckbox CreateCheckbox(); }\nclass WindowsUiFactory : IUiFactory\n{\n public IButton CreateButton() => new WindowsButton();\n public ICheckbox CreateCheckbox() => new WindowsCheckbox(); // guaranteed to match the button's style\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Abstract Factory pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/abstract-factory" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-024", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What's the actual structural difference between the Observer pattern and a general Publish-Subscribe (pub/sub) system, despite both being described as \"one-to-many notification\"?", "answer": "Classic Observer has subjects and observers with direct, if loosely-coupled, knowledge of each other's existence — the subject maintains a direct list of its registered observers and calls their notification method directly, and it's typically all happening within a single process, synchronously, with observers and subjects usually compiled together in the same codebase.\n\nA general pub/sub system introduces an intermediary (a message broker or event bus) between publishers and subscribers, so neither side ever holds a direct reference to the other at all — a publisher publishes to a named topic/channel with no idea who (if anyone) is subscribed, and the broker handles routing the message to every current subscriber, which commonly happens across process/service boundaries and asynchronously rather than as a direct, synchronous, in-process method call. Pub/sub is essentially Observer's underlying idea (interested parties get notified of events) generalized and decoupled further via that intermediary, extending the same core concept beyond a single process into a distributed, asynchronous setting.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Observer: subject holds observers directly, in-process, synchronous\nclass StockTicker { public event Action? PriceChanged; }\n\n// Pub/sub: neither side references the other; a broker routes messages\nawait messageBus.PublishAsync(\"stock.price.changed\", new PriceChangedEvent(101.5m));\n// elsewhere, in a different process:\nmessageBus.Subscribe(\"stock.price.changed\", e => Console.WriteLine(e.Price));" }, "reference": { "label": "Publish-Subscribe pattern — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/publisher-subscriber" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-025", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What over-abstraction risk does layering both Repository and Unit of Work on top of an ORM like EF Core specifically create, and when is that layering genuinely justified versus redundant?", "answer": "EF Core's `DbSet` already behaves very much like a repository (query and persist entities of a given type through a collection-like interface), and its `DbContext` already functions as a Unit of Work (tracking changes across multiple entity types and committing them together atomically on `SaveChanges()`) — wrapping a custom Repository/Unit of Work abstraction *around* EF Core, for a codebase that only ever uses EF Core and has no plan to swap it out, often just adds an extra layer of indirection that duplicates functionality the ORM already provides, without delivering the swappable-persistence-technology benefit the pattern is normally justified by.\n\nIt genuinely earns its keep when there's a real, concrete reason for the extra abstraction — a deliberate intent to support multiple, genuinely different persistence technologies behind the same interface, a need to fully isolate domain/business logic tests from any EF Core dependency at all (including EF Core's own in-memory provider, which itself has known behavioral quirks that don't perfectly match a real relational database), or a codebase where EF Core's specific querying idioms would otherwise leak pervasively throughout business logic in ways the team wants centrally contained. Absent one of those concrete reasons, it's a common, avoidable case of applying an architectural pattern out of habit rather than because it solves an actual problem the codebase has.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Often redundant: DbSet is already repository-shaped, DbContext already a Unit of Work\npublic class OrderService { private readonly AppDbContext _db; /* just use _db.Orders directly */ }\n\n// Justified: a genuine reason to isolate EF Core entirely\npublic interface IOrderRepository { Order? GetById(int id); }\npublic class InMemoryOrderRepository : IOrderRepository { /* fully EF-Core-free for fast unit tests */ }" }, "reference": { "label": "Infrastructure persistence layer design — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/infrastructure-persistence-layer-design" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-026", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What's the structural difference between the Decorator and Proxy patterns, given that both wrap an object behind the same interface?", "answer": "Structurally, Decorator and Proxy look nearly identical — both wrap an object implementing a shared interface and intercept calls to it — but their *intent* differs: Decorator exists specifically to add or extend behavior/responsibilities onto the wrapped object (and decorators are explicitly meant to be stacked, combining several independent behavior additions together in flexible combinations, like layering multiple coffee add-ons), while Proxy exists to *control access* to the wrapped object (lazy instantiation, permission checks, remote delegation) without changing or adding to what the object fundamentally does.\n\nIn practice, a Decorator generally always ends up actually delegating to and invoking the wrapped object's real behavior as part of doing its job (it's extending that behavior, so it needs to call it), whereas a protection Proxy might legitimately refuse to delegate to the real object at all (denying an unauthorized caller outright) — the distinction is more about the pattern's intended purpose and typical usage than any strict, enforceable structural difference between the two, which is exactly why the two are so often confused or conflated in practice.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface ICoffee { decimal Cost(); }\n\n// Decorator: extends behavior, always delegates through\nclass MilkDecorator : ICoffee { private readonly ICoffee _inner; public decimal Cost() => _inner.Cost() + 0.5m; public MilkDecorator(ICoffee i) => _inner = i; }\n\n// Proxy: controls access, may refuse to delegate at all\nclass AuthorizedCoffeeProxy : ICoffee\n{\n private readonly ICoffee _inner; private readonly bool _paid;\n public AuthorizedCoffeeProxy(ICoffee i, bool paid) { _inner = i; _paid = paid; }\n public decimal Cost() => _paid ? _inner.Cost() : throw new InvalidOperationException(\"Not paid\");\n}" }, "reference": { "label": "Decorator vs Proxy — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/decorator" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-027", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is a fluent interface, and how does the Builder pattern specifically rely on it as a technique?", "answer": "A fluent interface is an API design style where each method call returns the object itself (`this`/`self`) rather than `void` or an unrelated value, letting calls be chained together in a single, readable expression (`query.Where(...).OrderBy(...).Take(10)`) rather than requiring a separate statement and intermediate variable for each individual step.\n\nBuilder specifically relies on this technique to make its step-by-step construction API read naturally and clearly at the call site — `new PersonBuilder().WithName(\"Alex\").WithAge(30).Build()` reads almost like a sentence describing exactly what's being constructed, which is precisely the readability and self-documenting-call-site benefit Builder is meant to provide over an error-prone long parameter list;
