fluent interfaces aren't unique to Builder specifically (LINQ's method chaining is the same underlying technique applied to query composition rather than object construction), but Builder is one of the most common and canonical places the technique shows up.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Fluent interface: every call returns 'this' for chaining\nvar person = new PersonBuilder()\n .WithName(\"Alex\")\n .WithAge(30)\n .Build();\n\n// The same technique powers LINQ's method chaining\nvar result = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100).OrderBy(o => o.Date).Take(10);" }, "reference": { "label": "Fluent interface — Refactoring.Guru (Builder)", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/builder" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-028", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the Interpreter pattern, and why is it comparatively rarely used directly in application code despite being a classic GoF pattern?", "answer": "Interpreter defines a class-based representation for each grammar rule of a simple language (a mathematical expression grammar, a simple rules-engine syntax) and a way to \"interpret\" (evaluate) a sentence in that language by walking a tree of these rule objects — each grammar rule becomes a class implementing a common `Interpret(context)` method, and a complex expression is represented as a composed tree of these rule objects (which itself leans heavily on the Composite pattern structurally).\n\nIt's comparatively rare in everyday application code because hand-rolling a full class hierarchy this way scales poorly once the grammar being interpreted grows beyond something genuinely small and simple — for anything beyond a toy grammar, reaching for an existing parser-generator tool/library (or simply embedding an existing general-purpose scripting/expression language rather than inventing a new mini-language from scratch) is usually far more practical than hand-implementing and maintaining a full Interpreter-pattern class hierarchy; the pattern remains conceptually useful mainly for genuinely small, stable, narrowly-scoped grammars where a dedicated parser-generator tool would be overkill.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IExpression { int Interpret(); }\nclass Number : IExpression { private readonly int _v; public Number(int v) => _v = v; public int Interpret() => _v; }\nclass Add : IExpression\n{\n private readonly IExpression _l, _r;\n public Add(IExpression l, IExpression r) { _l = l; _r = r; }\n public int Interpret() => _l.Interpret() + _r.Interpret();\n}\n\nIExpression expr = new Add(new Number(3), new Number(4));\nConsole.WriteLine(expr.Interpret()); // 7 — fine for a tiny grammar, unwieldy for a real language" }, "reference": { "label": "Interpreter pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/interpreter" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-029", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is double dispatch, and how does the Visitor pattern rely on it to select the correct type-specific behavior at runtime?", "answer": "Ordinary method calls resolve to a specific overload based on a *single* runtime type — the receiving object's actual type, via normal virtual dispatch. Double dispatch is a technique for selecting behavior based on the runtime types of *two* objects involved in an interaction (both the element being visited and the specific visitor visiting it), which a single language-level virtual method call alone can't directly express, since a language's normal overload resolution for a method argument is typically decided by the argument's *static*, compile-time type, not its actual runtime type.\n\nVisitor achieves this by splitting the decision into two sequential virtual calls: the element's `Accept(visitor)` method is dispatched virtually based on the element's actual runtime type (dispatch #1), and inside that method, it calls `visitor.Visit(this)` — passing itself with its now-known-concrete static type (since `this` inside that specific overridden `Accept` method has a statically-known concrete type), letting the compiler correctly resolve which specific overloaded `Visit` method to call on the visitor (dispatch #2). The combination of these two single-dispatch calls in sequence achieves what amounts to dispatch based on both objects' concrete types together.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "interface IVisitor { void Visit(Circle c); void Visit(Square s); }\ninterface IShape { void Accept(IVisitor v); }\n\nclass Circle : IShape\n{\n public void Accept(IVisitor v) => v.Visit(this); // dispatch #1: virtual, by Circle's runtime type\n // inside Accept, 'this' is statically known as Circle, so...\n}\n// ...dispatch #2: overload resolution picks Visit(Circle) at compile time inside Accept" }, "reference": { "label": "Visitor pattern — Refactoring.Guru", "url": "https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/visitor" } }, { "id": "q-designpattern-030", "category": "Design Patterns", "question": "What is the God Object anti-pattern, and how does it typically emerge gradually from otherwise reasonable-looking incremental decisions?", "answer": "A God Object is a single class that has accumulated far too many responsibilities — it knows about and coordinates large portions of the system, has an enormous number of methods and dependencies, and becomes the class everyone has to touch (and risk breaking something unrelated) for almost any change, violating the Single Responsibility Principle at an extreme scale.\n\nIt rarely gets created deliberately all at once — it typically accretes gradually, one individually reasonable-looking decision at a time: \"this new piece of logic is closely related to what `OrderManager` already does, so I'll just add it here\" repeated many times over a codebase's life, with nobody along the way stepping back to notice the *cumulative* effect of many locally-sensible additions landing in the same already-overloaded class. It's closely related to the Anemic Domain Model anti-pattern from the opposite direction — where a God Object hoards too much *behavior*, an Anemic Domain Model instead strips domain objects of nearly all behavior (reducing them to plain data holders) while pushing all actual logic into separate, disconnected \"service\" or \"manager\" classes that operate on that data from outside, both representing a failure to distribute responsibility appropriately across a system's classes.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Accretes one \"reasonable\" addition at a time...\nclass OrderManager\n{\n public void PlaceOrder() { }\n public void SendEmail() { } // \"closely related enough\"\n public void UpdateInventory() { } // \"closely related enough\"\n public void GenerateInvoicePdf() { } // \"closely related enough\"\n public void LogAuditTrail() { } // ...until it does everything\n}\n\n// Fix: split by responsibility, same as the SRP example\nclass OrderService { public void PlaceOrder() { } }\nclass InvoiceService { public void GenerateInvoicePdf() { } }" }, "reference": { "label": "Single Responsibility Principle — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/architectural-principles#single-responsibility" } }, { "id": "q-security-001", "category": "Security", "question": "What is the OWASP Top 10 and why does it matter?", "answer": "The OWASP Top 10 is a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks, published by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. It covers categories like broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, and security misconfiguration.\n\nIt matters because it gives teams a shared, prioritized vocabulary for risk: instead of chasing every possible vulnerability, engineers and security reviewers can focus effort on the classes of bugs that account for the vast majority of real-world breaches, and use it as a checklist during design reviews and code review.", "reference": { "label": "OWASP Top 10", "url": "https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/" } }, { "id": "q-security-002", "category": "Security", "question": "What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?", "answer": "SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated directly into a SQL query, letting an attacker alter the query's structure — for example entering `' OR '1'='1` to bypass a login check, or appending a second statement to delete data.\n\nPrevention is primarily parameterized queries / prepared statements (or an ORM that uses them under the hood), so user input is always treated as data, never as executable SQL. Secondary defenses include least-privilege database accounts, input validation, and avoiding dynamic SQL string building entirely where possible.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Vulnerable — string concatenation\nvar sql = \"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = '\" + userInput + \"'\";\n\n// Safe — parameterized query\nvar cmd = new SqlCommand(\"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = @name\", connection);\ncmd.Parameters.AddWithValue(\"@name\", userInput); // treated as data, never as SQL" }, "reference": { "label": "SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP", "url": "https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" } }, { "id": "q-security-003", "category": "Security", "question": "What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and what are its main types?", "answer": "XSS is an injection attack where an attacker gets malicious JavaScript to execute in another user's browser session, typically by injecting a `" }, "reference": { "label": "Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — OWASP", "url": "https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/xss/" } }, { "id": "q-security-004", "category": "Security", "question": "How do you defend against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?", "answer": "The core defense is context-aware output encoding — escape data based on where it lands (HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript, URL, CSS) rather than using one generic escape function everywhere.\n\nOn top of that: use frameworks that auto-escape by default (React, Angular) and avoid dangerous APIs like `innerHTML` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` unless the content is sanitized; set a Content-Security-Policy to restrict script sources as defense in depth; mark cookies `HttpOnly` so injected scripts can't read them; and validate/sanitize any input that is later rendered as rich HTML (e.g. with a library like DOMPurify).", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": "\n

{userInput}

\n\n\n
\n\n\n\n" }, "reference": { "label": "Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP", "url": "https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" } }, { "id": "q-security-005", "category": "Security", "question": "What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and how is it mitigated?", "answer": "CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting an unwanted request to a site they're authenticated with — for example an `` or auto-submitting form on an attacker's page that fires a POST to `/transfer-funds`, relying on the browser automatically attaching the victim's session cookie.\n\nMitigations: anti-CSRF tokens (a random value tied to the session, required on state-changing requests and unreadable by other origins), the `SameSite` cookie attribute (`Lax` or `Strict`) to stop cookies being sent on cross-site requests, and requiring re-authentication or custom headers for sensitive actions, since simple cross-site forms can't set custom headers.", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": "\n
\n \n
\n\n\n\n" }, "reference": { "label": "Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP", "url": "https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" } }, { "id": "q-security-006", "category": "Security", "question": "What is the difference between authentication and authorization?", "answer": "Authentication (AuthN) answers \"who are you?\" — verifying identity, typically via a password, token, or biometric factor.\n\nAuthorization (AuthZ) answers \"what are you allowed to do?\" — deciding whether an already-authenticated identity has permission to perform a specific action or access a specific resource. Authentication must happen first; authorization decisions are then made per request, often using roles, claims, or policies.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Authentication — who are you?\nvar result = await signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(username, password, false, false);\n\n// Authorization — what are you allowed to do?\n[Authorize(Roles = \"Admin\")] // checked only after authentication has already established identity\npublic IActionResult DeleteUser(int id) => Ok();" }, "reference": { "label": "Authentication vs. Authorization — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/" } }, { "id": "q-security-007", "category": "Security", "question": "What is the difference between hashing and encryption?", "answer": "Hashing is a one-way transformation: a hash function maps input of any size to a fixed-size output, and there is no practical way to reverse it back to the original input. It's used for integrity checks and password storage, where you never need to recover the original value — only compare hashes.\n\nEncryption is two-way: data is transformed with a key so it can later be decrypted back to the original plaintext using that same key (symmetric) or a paired key (asymmetric). It's used when the original data must eventually be recovered, such as protecting data at rest or in transit.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Hashing — one-way, for integrity/password checks\nvar hash = SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(password)); // never reversible\n\n// Encryption — two-way, recoverable with the key\nusing var aes = Aes.Create();\nvar ciphertext = aes.EncryptCbc(plaintext, iv); // can be decrypted back with the same key" }, "reference": { "label": "Cryptography Model — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/security/cryptography-model" } }, { "id": "q-security-008", "category": "Security", "question": "Why should passwords be salted, and why should you use a slow hash like bcrypt or Argon2 instead of SHA-256?", "answer": "A salt is random data unique per user, stored alongside the hash and combined with the password before hashing. It defeats precomputed rainbow-table attacks and ensures two users with the same password get different stored hashes.\n\nGeneric fast hashes like SHA-256 are designed for speed, which is exactly the wrong property for password storage — it lets an attacker with a stolen hash dump try billions of guesses per second on cheap hardware. Bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 are deliberately slow and (for scrypt/Argon2) memory-hard, incorporate salting internally, and expose a cost factor you can tune upward over time as hardware gets faster, making brute-forcing dramatically more expensive.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Vulnerable to rainbow tables and fast brute-forcing\nvar hash = SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(password));\n\n// Correct — salted internally, deliberately slow, tunable cost factor\nvar hash2 = BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.HashPassword(password, workFactor: 12);\nbool valid = BCrypt.Net.BCrypt.Verify(password, hash2);" }, "reference": { "label": "Password Storage Cheat Sheet — OWASP", "url": "https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html" } }, { "id": "q-security-009", "category": "Security", "question": "What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?", "answer": "Symmetric encryption (e.g. AES) uses the same secret key to both encrypt and decrypt. It's fast and efficient for large amounts of data, but every party that needs to decrypt must securely share that one key — key distribution is the hard problem.\n\nAsymmetric encryption (e.g. RSA, ECC) uses a key pair: a public key that anyone can use to encrypt or verify, and a private key kept secret by the owner used to decrypt or sign. It solves the key-distribution problem but is computationally much slower, which is why in practice protocols like TLS use asymmetric encryption to securely exchange a symmetric session key, then switch to symmetric encryption for the actual data.", "snippet": { "language": "csharp", "code": "// Symmetric — same key both ways, fast\nusing var aes = Aes.Create();\nvar ciphertext = aes.EncryptCbc(data, iv);\n\n// Asymmetric — public key encrypts, private key decrypts\nusing var rsa = RSA.Create();\nvar encrypted = rsa.Encrypt(data, RSAEncryptionPadding.OaepSHA256); // slower, solves key distribution" }, "reference": { "label": "Symmetric and Asymmetric Cryptography — Microsoft Learn", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/security/cryptographic-services" } }, { "id": "q-security-010", "category": "Security", "question": "What happens during a TLS handshake, at a high level?", "answer": "The client and server first agree on a TLS version and cipher suite. The server presents its certificate, which the client validates against a trusted certificate authority chain to confirm it's talking to the real server (and not a man-in-the-middle).\n\nThey then perform a key exchange (commonly ephemeral Diffie-Hellman in modern TLS) to derive a shared symmetric session key without ever transmitting it directly. From that point on, all traffic is encrypted and integrity-protected with that symmetric key, which is far cheaper than using asymmetric crypto for every message.", "snippet": { "language": "text", "code": "1. ClientHello / ServerHello — agree on TLS version + cipher suite\n2. Server presents its certificate — client validates against a trusted CA chain\n3. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange — derives a shared symmetric session key\n4. All further traffic encrypted with that fast symmetric key, not the slower asymmetric keys" }, "reference": { "label": "Transport Layer Security (TLS) — MDN", "url": "https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/TLS" } }, { "id": "q-security-011", "category": "Security", "question": "What is Content Security Policy (CSP) and what problem does it solve?", "answer": "CSP is an HTTP response header that lets a server declare which sources of scripts, styles, images, fonts, and other resources a browser is allowed to load and execute for that page, e.g. `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' cdn.example.com`.\n\nIt's primarily a defense-in-depth layer against XSS: even if an attacker manages to inject a `\n

'tracked!');" }, "reference": { "label": "Reactivity in Depth — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/reactivity-in-depth.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-003", "category": "Vue", "question": "reference": { "label": "Single-File Components — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/sfc.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-005", "category": "Vue", "question": "How does v-model work under the hood in Vue?", "answer": "`v-model` is syntactic sugar for binding a value and listening for an update event together — on a native input it expands roughly to `:value=\"x\" @input=\"x = $event.target.value\"`, and on a custom component it binds a `modelValue` prop and listens for an `update:modelValue` event by convention (in Vue 3).\n\nBecause it's just sugar over that prop/event pair, a custom component can support `v-model` by explicitly defining a `modelValue` prop and emitting `update:modelValue` — and Vue 3 allows multiple named `v-model` bindings on the same component (`v-model:title`, `v-model:content`) for components that need to two-way bind more than one value.", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": "\n\n\n\n\n" }, "reference": { "label": "Component v-model — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/components/v-model.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-006", "category": "Vue", "question": "What's the difference between a computed property, a method, and a watcher in Vue?", "answer": "A computed property derives a value from reactive dependencies and is cached — it only recalculates when one of its underlying dependencies actually changes, making it efficient for values referenced multiple times in a template. A method called from the template re-runs on every single re-render regardless of whether its inputs changed, since there's no caching involved.\n\nA watcher doesn't return a derived value at all — it runs a side effect in response to a specific reactive value changing (like making an API call whenever a search query changes), which is the right tool when you need to react to a change rather than just compute a new display value from it.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "const fullName = computed(() => `${first.value} ${last.value}`); // cached, recomputes only on dependency change\n\nfunction getFullName() { return `${first.value} ${last.value}`; } // re-runs every render, no caching\n\nwatch(searchQuery, (newQuery) => fetchResults(newQuery)); // side effect, not a derived value" }, "reference": { "label": "Computed Properties — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/computed.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-007", "category": "Vue", "question": "What's the difference between v-if and v-show in Vue?", "answer": "`v-if` conditionally adds or completely removes the element (and its component, if any) from the DOM — when false, the element and any associated component lifecycle simply don't exist, which has a real (if usually small) cost each time it toggles since Vue has to create/destroy the element.\n\n`v-show` always keeps the element in the DOM and merely toggles its CSS `display` property — cheaper for elements that toggle frequently, since there's no destroy/recreate cost, but it means any associated component logic keeps running even while hidden. The rule of thumb: `v-show` for things that toggle often, `v-if` for things that are conditionally rendered rarely or that should genuinely not exist when false.", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": " \n " }, "reference": { "label": "v-if vs v-show — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/conditional.html#v-if-vs-v-show" } }, { "id": "q-vue-008", "category": "Vue", "question": "Why does the key attribute matter when using v-for to render a list in Vue?", "answer": "The `key` gives Vue a stable identity for each item in a list, letting its diffing algorithm correctly match old and new list items to reuse, move, or remove the correct underlying DOM nodes and component instances — rather than falling back to matching purely by list position.\n\nUsing the array index as the key (a common shortcut) breaks this when the list is reordered, filtered, or has items inserted/removed from the middle — Vue can end up reusing the wrong component instance for the wrong data, which is especially dangerous when list items contain their own local state (like a text input), since that state can end up attached to the wrong row after a reorder.", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": "\n

This one-directional \"props down, events up\" pattern keeps data flow predictable and traceable, avoiding the harder-to-follow bugs that come from a child silently mutating its parent's state directly.", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": "\n\n\n\n" }, "reference": { "label": "Props — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/components/props.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-010", "category": "Vue", "question": "What problem does provide/inject solve in Vue?", "answer": "Passing data through many layers of nested components purely via props (\"prop drilling\") means every intermediate component has to accept and re-pass a prop it doesn't actually use itself, just so a distant descendant can eventually receive it.\n\n`provide` lets an ancestor component make a value available to any descendant, and `inject` lets that descendant pull it directly, regardless of how many intermediate layers sit between them — skipping the prop-drilling chain entirely. It's best suited for genuinely cross-cutting concerns (like a theme or a shared service) rather than as a general substitute for normal props, since it makes data flow less explicit/traceable than props.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "// Ancestor\nprovide(\"theme\", ref(\"dark\")); // available to any descendant, however deep\n\n// Distant descendant — no prop drilling through every layer in between\nconst theme = inject(\"theme\");" }, "reference": { "label": "Provide / Inject — Vue.js docs", "url": "https://vuejs.org/guide/components/provide-inject.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-011", "category": "Vue", "question": "What is a Vue slot, and how does it compare to React's children prop or Angular's content projection?", "answer": "A slot lets a parent component inject template content into a designated placeholder inside a child component's own template (``), similar in spirit to React's `props.children` or Angular's `` — all three solve the same underlying problem of letting a reusable wrapper component accept arbitrary content from its parent.\n\nVue's slots go further with named slots (multiple distinct injection points in one component) and scoped slots (where the child passes data back to the parent's slot content, letting the parent customize how child-owned data is rendered) — a level of flexibility React's children prop doesn't natively provide without additional patterns like render props.", "snippet": { "language": "html", "code": "\n

Vuex is still supported for existing projects, but Pinia is the default choice for new ones.", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "// Pinia — actions can mutate state directly, no separate mutations concept\nexport const useCartStore = defineStore(\"cart\", {\n state: () => ({ items: [] }),\n actions: {\n add(item) { this.items.push(item); }, // no commit() needed, unlike Vuex mutations\n },\n});" }, "reference": { "label": "Pinia documentation", "url": "https://pinia.vuejs.org/" } }, { "id": "q-vue-013", "category": "Vue", "question": "What are navigation guards in Vue Router, and what are they used for?", "answer": "Navigation guards are functions that run at defined points during route navigation — globally (`router.beforeEach`), per-route, or within a component — letting you intercept, redirect, or cancel a navigation before it completes.\n\nCommon uses mirror Angular's route guards: blocking access to a route unless the user is authenticated, checking role-based permissions before entering an admin section, or confirming with the user before navigating away from a form with unsaved changes (via an in-component guard like `beforeRouteLeave`).", "snippet": { "language": "javascript", "code": "router.beforeEach((to, from) => {\n if (to.meta.requiresAuth && !isLoggedIn()) {\n return { name: \"login\" }; // redirect, cancelling the original navigation\n }\n});\n\n// In-component:\nonBeforeRouteLeave(() => confirm(\"Discard unsaved changes?\"));" }, "reference": { "label": "Navigation Guards — Vue Router docs", "url": "https://router.vuejs.org/guide/advanced/navigation-guards.html" } }, { "id": "q-vue-014", "category": "Vue", "question": "What does \n" }, "reference": { "label": "
